speakerposition: Minister for External Relations; Minister responsible for La Francophonie
subsubtopic: MINISTER'S STATEMENT ON VISIT TO ASIA
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am eager to share with the House what I have seen and experienced during the past couple of weeks as I travelled in China and Thailand. I say "eager" because I believe our relationship with the new Asia, which is emerging with astonishing speed, is crucial to our mutual interests.

After visiting several parts of Asia and a series of development co-operation projects in which Canada is involved, I am very pleased to say I was given tangible proof of the effectiveness of our development aid. The projects in which Canada is involved are having a definite impact.
Last week during my visit to Thailand, I signed several agreements aimed at promoting co-operation in major sectors between our two countries. For instance, Canada will provide a grant of $5 million to help the women of Thailand participate to a greater extent in the development of their country. These funds will enable them to initiate income-generating activities, open small businesses, have access to credit and receive leadership training.
Other agreements concern the funding of Canadian goods and services; scholarships for Thai students who want to pursue post-secondary studies in Canada in crucial areas such as energy and food production; and opening up new areas for co-operation such as food processing, air traffic control and environmental protection.
I visited the Champthai factory, an example of a joint venture involving a Canadian company, Champion Road Machinery of Goderich, Ontario and a Thai company. I visited a centre for remote sensing which is receiving technical assistance from Canadian companies in Montreal and Vancouver.
I was profoundly affected by my visit to a school for the blind, where fantastic work is being done.
I also went to Northeast Thailand, the country's poorest region, where I visited rural development projects funded by Canada. However, what struck me most was the way the relationship between our two countries has changed. There is so much vitality and growth everywhere in Thailand, and there are so many positive aspects for Canada that we can no longer properly speak of a donor-beneficiary relationship. These terms reflect a dependence that is no longer significant.

I can report that the same is true, but on a larger scale, in our relationship with China. It was a great privilege to spend 10 days in the world's most populous nation as a representative of the Canadian Government. It was a very productive 10 days, indeed. There were meetings with Deng Xiaoing, China's elder statesman, with the President, the Prime Minister and other officials at the highest level.
In following up on the Prime Minister's commitment of last year, I was able to announce, as Minister responsible for CIDA, 11 new projects of development co-operation to a value of over $90 million in such fields as management education, municipal planning and linkages at the college and university level. I was happy with the focus of our existing program, which The Globe and Mail has described as aimed at people and knowledge. I am particularly pleased to report that we have also taken some early initiatives in the important and promising fields of transportation and telecommunications.
There were many highlights. On one occasion I met with representatives of one of our development partners, the AllChina Women's Federation, doubtless the world's largest such organization with 93 million members. On another occasion I travelled by boat on the Yangtze to the site of the proposed Three Gorges Complex where the river, the hills and the mists truly speak to the soul. However, this spot is also where China is contemplating building a power complex with a capacity greater than the entire James Bay Development. The proposed project would also control floods and extend river navigation. We can be proud that China has entrusted a Canadian consortium with the carrying out of the feasibility study. We can only assist China, in its great wisdom, to make this crucial decision about its future.
There are two further observations I would like to offer. The first concerns Asia in general. Asia is changing fast-much faster, 1 fear, than our Canadian ideas and attitudes about

Asian reality. The fact is that Asia with immense needs, pent up demand, a large and growing middle class and huge human and material resources, will become the mainstream, the centre of gravity of the global economy in the very near future-likely by the turn of the century, less than 5,000 days from now. It will have the world's largest, most diverse and, perhaps, most modern industrial capacity. This means that our relationship with Asia will be utterly transformed.
In reality, of course, transformations do not happen overnight-they are already well advanced. Some of us gained that insight when we recently saw Canadian communities vying for investment by Japanese and Korean car makers. But I am very concerned that Canadian perceptions are lagging dangerously far behind the fast pace of change. How many of us have looked recently at GNP per capita figures and noticed how Asian countries have begun to surpass those in Europe? At current growth rates for per capita income Taiwan and Korea will be richer than the United States four decades from now.
The point I want to make is that if Canadians want a strategy for success, whether we are talking about government, business or Canadians in general, they had better realize that, especially in Asia, the old game is over and a quite different one is under way with new roles and new rules. It is important for Canada as a whole to understand the new reality so that our country can make major adjustments, economically, politically and psychologically.

One of the aspects of this new reality is the fact that we need China more than it needs us. A look at the total volume of our exports in 1985 reveals that China accounted for 3.4 per cent, whereas Canada was the origin of only 1.6 per cent of Chinese imports. At that time, we turned a new page of Canadian economic history when, for the first time, a larger volume of our exports went to the Pacific region instead of crossing the Atlantic.
If we expect Canada to prosper as a major trading nation we must gain a very clear insight into worldwide economic events and do everything we can to cultivate our ties with Asia. We must establish a long-term economic and institutional relationship.
More subjective, my second remark has to do with the state of our relations with Asia and the way the Government approachesThis significant aspect of our external relations. In this respect I can say that our relations are excellent and that the Government is taking decisive action to strengthen these ties with Asia well into the XXIth century. Everywhere I went I was struck by the people's warm and friendly reception.
Although Canada does not rank high in terms of population, our impact in China is much more important than most of us would imagine. Our reputation over there is practically second to none. The name of Dr. Bethune was on everyone's lips.
I also believe that their attitude towards us is due in part to the deep respect which Canada has always shown for China and its priorities. Indeed, the same things goes for Thailand.
By any means the Government does not neglect any opportunity to expand these ties. I have just returned from my visit over there with the Governor General. The Minister of Communications (Miss MacDonald) as well travelled to that country a few days ago, and recently there were other ministerial visits.

While in Asia I had the opportunity to sign a number of agreements for specific projects, thus moving our co-operation forward in keeping with, for instance, the commitments made last year by the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney). To further the process, Cabinet has now approved a strategy for China which reflects the importance Canada attaches to its relations with the Asia-Pacific region in general and with China in particular.
The strategy builds upon the major achievements since Canada's recognition of the People's Republic of China in 1970, especially the measures taken by the Government in the past two years, such as the opening of a consulate in Shanghai and the announcement by the Prime Minister when he visited Beijing last May that Canada is doubling its CIDA bilateral program and setting up a concessional financing facility. The strategy is designed to set an institutional framework for the building of a focused, orchestrated and dynamic approach to our relationship with China, a key political actor in Asia and Canada's fifth largest market in the world.
To conclude, Mr. Speaker, I wish to share with you a Thai tradition. When one gives alms to a monk it is then customary to thank the monk for accepting the gift. The truth is that Canada's participation in Asia's development is indeed enriching and benefiting Canada. Day by day the relationship between our country, and those of Asia, grows more balanced and becomes more mutually beneficial.

subsubtopic: MINISTER'S STATEMENT ON VISIT TO ASIA
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, first, I want to say that I wish that my comments on the Minister's presentation could be better prepared, since I think it has been a valuable contribution. Unfortunately, I was not in receipt of her remarks and was therefore unable to give time to the preparation of the type of remarks that I would like to make on behalf of my Party. At the same time, on behalf of the Members of the House, I wish to thank the Minister for the fact that she has come to the House to report on her visit and to give us an insight into her findings.
As an aside, an interesting aspect of her remarks was her comment concerning the importance of the trade future of the Pacific Rim. The growth of the power of many of the previously undeveloped and now rapidly developing countries in Asia will in fact shift Canada's trade to a larger extent to the Pacific Rim as opposed to the Atlantic Region, which is an idea that Canadians have to catch up with, as the Minister has indicated. Now that she has come back, the Minister should
April 2, 1987

now meet with the Minister for International Trade (Miss Carney) for the purpose of enlightening that Minister, as she is contemplating Canada's trade relations with the United States, on the importance of trade with the nations of the Pacific Rim. It is our contention that it is within the total context of our GATT relations and within the context of our total trade with all of the nations of the world that we should consider our trade relations with the United States. Perhaps the Minister for External Relations will be helpful in getting that point across to the Minister for International Trade.
I should like to call attention to the Minister's report on Thailand. Given that she is the Minister for External Relations, her report includes a section on the work of CIDA, something that is entirely within her area of responsibility. In looking at our development programs, both multilateral and bilateral, we want to ensure that such programs are beneficial to the poorest people of the countries involved. In addition, we want to ensure that any such developments are not in any way harmful to the weak and the poor of those countries. This, of course, is something that is difficult to achieve when one is dealing with sovereign nations. Certainly, we would not want them to feel that we were interfering with their plans and their views. At the same time, Mr. Speaker, we do have that responsibility of which I spoke.
I was pleased to hear that the Minister went to the poorer sections in Thailand and had the opportunity to see what some of those problems are. But, it does also raise certain areas of concern, those concerns having to do with the plight of the poorer people in these countries and the whole question of human rights. I regret that the Minister did not make a few comments in that regard.
Like everyone else, I was happy to hear about the desire to provide education and to work on co-operative educational programs with Thailand, including the exchange of students, the possibility of having Thai students in Canada-something which would be beneficial to both of our countries. Such programs are a positive step in beginning the process of improving human rights in other countries and in ameliorating the suffering that takes place in those countries.
I was pleased to hear about the Minister's visit to China, a country which we often speak of as the "Sleeping Giant". Given the vastness of that country, and the size of its population, it is certainly a good thing to have Canadians generally visit that country to acquaint themselves with it, and it is particularly beneficial when leading members of our Cabinet travel to that very important nation. While it is a Communist nation, it is an important one, and Canada has provided leadership in the past in opening up relations with it. In this regard, I make reference to former Prime Minister Trudeau, who helped create a better respect for China as a nation that must be dealt with in the realities of the world. So, it is a good thing that the Minister was able to spend time in China,
Statements by Ministers
allowing her to return to Canada with a better assessment and appreciation of things in that country.
I should like again to call the attention of the Minister to the manner in which we provide aid to these countries. As the Minister responsible for CIDA, she will be aware that some of the projects undertaken around the world have led to some tragic results. We have had examples of countries, with the assistance of the International World Bank and the IMF, going after major projects, including the construction of hydroelectric dams, that have led to tragic consequences. We have had examples where a nation's leaders, in their desire to keep up with the progress of other countries, have embarked on projects which, while providing them with some personal glory, have done a great deal of damage to the country's population.
I will not cite specifics. I think the Minister knows what I am talking about. Certainly in various nations of Africa, this kind of thing has taken place.
I can understand that the Minister, in speaking about the Three Gorges Complex, would not want to insult the leadership of the Chinese people by challenging them about the wisdom of that project. However, it is a project in which we are involved, and a project on which Canadian firms are seeking contracts. The construction of hydro-electric dams in other areas of the world have led to the displacement of entire populations, with no provision for relocating the people affected or providing them with a better and improved way of life. On the contrary, such projects have oftentimes led to the total destruction of the lives of those people. Oftentimes, they result in economic ruin. In addition, there have often been, as a longer range result, dreadful environmental repercussions.
By no means am I suggesting to the Minister that all hydroelectric dams are bad. On the contrary, provided that all of the necessary safeguards are taken, they can be good. However, we have seen ourselves involved in projects where not enough attention has been given to these matters, with the result that, instead of having brought about alleviation of the suffering of the poor, we have in fact brought about just the opposite. Many projects bring about very dubious long range benefits for the economy of the country involved, with very powerful and tragic short term repercussions on the people directly affected by the project. I regret that the Minister did not comment on how some of these tragedies of the past could be avoided insofar as any involvement we have with China is concerned.
We have to ask ourselves, too, just how the Minister sees her role as one who is concerned with developments. Development, of course, does include trade, and certainly it is not her function to try to be the Minister for International Trade. However, I think her observations on the trade situation will be of assistance to her colleagues in Cabinet. I would welcome from the Minister, as soon as possible, a further detailed explanation as to what is happening in Asia insofar as the poorer people are concerned, those on whom we are supposedly focusing as our top priority in terms of CIDA aid.

Indeed, in the Minister's statement-and I appreciate that in a short presentation such as this she cannot cover everything-I did miss hearing anything about the tragic fact that there are so many people on the Asian continent who continue to live in very limited circumstances, people who are illiterate and not well cared for medically. These are the very people, through our CIDA operations, we want to help.
As well, I should like to have heard her observations on nongovernmental organizations, organizations that monitor the human rights situation and the economic situation in those countries. I hope that she did visit some such organizations.
My comments, Mr. Speaker, are meant to constitute both congratulations to the Minister and an expression of concern in relation to those areas that were omitted from her remarks. I do want to express my appreciation to the Minister for her having taken the time to make this trip and for the courtesy of her report to the House.

subsubtopic: MINISTER'S STATEMENT ON VISIT TO ASIA
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on behalf of my Party I wish to express appreciation to the Hon. Minister for External Relations (Mrs. Landry) for her statement and for the trip which she made, along with the Governor General and others, to China and Thailand. The growing importance of Asia in the world and in Canada's relationships with other parts of the world has been underscored by the visit and by the Minister's report.
In the early 1950s the question of the recognition of the People's Republic of China was something of an United Church heresy, because the United Church of Canada was
April 2, 1987

advocating that before many other organizations in Canada were. Some people felt that the sky would fall in if Canada took such a drastic step. It finally happened in 1970, and since then there have been absolutely no regrets on the part of Canada that we have recognized the People's Republic of China. We have been seeking to build stronger ties ever since. It is important, as the Minister has done, to underscore the importance of those ties both for Canada and for the world in general. Coming from a riding on the Pacific Coast, I know how important it is for our people.
China is a country which has made tremendous strides in the last few years, yet it continues to face tremendous problems. Canadian and Chinese co-operation is essential and, as the Minister pointed out, it is essential for Canada as well as for countries in Asia. I was very pleased to note in the Minister's comments on Thailand that we are moving beyond the donor-recipient relationship. It is important for us to move into an era of international co-operation rather than see a kind of paternalistic relationship continuing.
I have some concerns about some of the issues mentioned by the Minister, certainly the major dam project. It is interesting to note that we have announced an additional $1.4 million to expand the scope of the Three Gorges feasibility study. This is in addition to the $8.7 million contract awarded last July to a Canadian consortium. That contract was to look at the technical, economic, and financial viability of a multi-purpose development in the Three Gorges. When we are considering a project of this kind, it is important to be aware of the environmental impact and of the human rights impact-what will be the results on people upstream and downstream from the developments. While we recognize that the final decision will be that of the Chinese Government-and its integrity as a Government is involved-and that Canada is involved in providing financial assistance, we have a responsibility to ensure that some values which are very important to Canadians in terms of the environment and human rights values are being protected or looked after. Before any further contracts are let involving Canadian money for the Three Gorges project, I urge upon the Minister that there be some statement to Canadians about the environmental impact and about the human rights impact of this massive development.
The Minister knows, as do all Members of the House, that sometimes massive developments which can produce some very positive results can also have some very negative results. Every Government must be involved in trying to weigh what is positive against what is negative. That is the final responsibility of the Chinese Government as far as the project is concerned, but I think the Canadian Government has a responsibility in terms of further Canadian assistance.
Statements by Ministers
I was pleased to see an emphasis in the Minister's statement on assistance to women and the $5 million which will be going to women's projects in Thailand to help them develop income generating projects. It is a helpful emphasis. We want to underscore the need for CIDA constantly to find ways of emphasizing the needs of women around the world.
This brings me to a concern that there is no dollar figure attached to the support for the All China Women's Federation. The Minister pointed out that its membership is 93 million, a huge organization, yet there is no dollar figure attached to the kind of aid which will be going to it. Perhaps the dollar figures will come later. I hope they will. It is very important not to lose sight of this as we emphasize the importance of women. It has an important public relations aspect for Canadians. They want to hear about it, but they would also like to hear what dollar figures are attached.
The Minister's remarks about the changes which are taking place in Asia are well taken, yet she talked about a strategy for Canadian success in that huge and developing market. I am not completely sure what is our strategy for success, but I have a suspicion that the Minister is trying to have a closer link between Canadian development assistance and Canadian trade, and that bothers me. Development assistance has its own priorities which must stand on their own and be addressed on their own. Time after time, talking about development assistance, representations have been made to the Government that the primary target for such assistance should be the poorest of the poor. Yet Canada has traditionally had a policy of tied aid by which we seek to do two things; we hope to help developing countries and that somehow we help the poor, and we are also very concerned about developing Canadian industry, exports and services.
O)
I do not think the best way to encourage Canadian trade and services is by trying to use development assistance as a lever. These two very commendable goals have to stand on their own, and when we try to use tied aid as a method of levering our way into a market, no matter how important that market is, we end up having some very skewed development projects. We have seen some of the white elephants that have been created by tied aid in other parts of the world. This should not be done on a continuing basis. Trade has its own priorities. We should be addressing it in a straightforward, honest manner, and we should be addressing development priorities in a straightforward, honest manner. I leave those comments with the Minister and with the House.
Again, I thank the Minister for her statement. I want to underscore the importance of her visit, and the visit by other Canadian Ministers and other Canadians generally to the whole Asian area.

subsubtopic: OPPOSITION TO PROPOSED CHANGES TO PATENT ACT
speechtext: Madam Speaker, 1 have the honour, pursuant to Standing Order 106, of tabling a petition signed by residents of the riding of Saint-Michel-Ahuntsic who object to the proposed changes to the Patent Act in Bill C-22. They feel the Government's proposal will increase the already high cost of provincial health insurance plans and will also have a direct impact on all Canadians not covered by private insurance plans. The undersigned call upon Parliament to reject this proposal which will increase the price of drugs for all Canadians.

subsubtopic: REQUEST FOR INCREASED GOVERNMENT AID TO CO-OP HOUSING PROGRAMS
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I have another petition, which I have the honour and the privilege of tabling on behalf of my constituents. It is signed by people in my riding who object to the Government's decision to make substantial changes in Canada's housing policy. In this International Year of Shelter for the Homeless, they feel that the Government's definition of essential needs is preventing hundreds of thousands of Canadians living below the poverty line from receiving Government housing assistance.
Wherefore the undersigned humbly pray and call upon Parliament to immediately increase funding for the Cooperative Housing Program.

subsubtopic: OPPOSITION TO PROPOSED CHANGES TO PATENT ACT
speechtext:
My last petition is again signed by people from the riding of Saint-Michel-Ahuntsic who object to the proposed changes to the
Patent Act in Bill C-22. The undersigned are advising me of their objections because they feel the Government's proposal will increase the already high cost of provincial health insurance plans, considering the fact that the provinces pay 65 per cent of all drug costs.
The undersigned therefore call upon Parliament to reject these proposals which will increase the price of drugs for all Canadians.

subsubtopic: OPPOSITION TO PROPOSED CHANGES TO PATENT ACT
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I have the honour to present a petition from a number of residents in Newfoundland protesting the Government's changes to the Patent Act. Whereas the proposed changes to the Patent Act will directly affect all Canadians who are not protected by private or governmental medicare programs, and whereas the Government's proposal would raise the cost, already high, of provincial health care programs, and whereas the proposed changes to the Patent Act are another example of the Canadian Government's concessions in free trade negotiations with the United States at the expense of every day Canadians, the petitioners humbly pray and call upon Parliament to reject these proposals which will increase prescription drug prices to Canadians.
I have another petition from residents of Hull and from different parts of the Province of Quebec and from as far East as Moncton and Dieppe, New Brunswick. They too say that the monopoly granted to innovative pharmaceutical companies will prevent competition from generic companies and will result in an increase in drug costs and prices which will severely restrict the ability of average Canadians to buy necessary prescription drugs, and that the proposed changes to the Patent Act are another example of the Canadian Government's concessions in free trade negotiations with the United States at the expense of everyday Canadians.
I have a further petition on the same subject, Madam Speaker, from residents of the Province of Quebec, Carleton, St. Omer, Nouvelle and so on. They protest the Government's action in presenting Bill C-22, the Patent Act, and are very much against it. They recognize that Bill C-22 will increase prices to the poor, to ordinary Canadians, senior citizens and those who can least afford it in our society. They ask that this House condemn the Minister and this Bill. They ask the Government to defer and, indeed, scrap this legislation.

Therefore, they humbly pray and call upon Parliament to reject these proposals which will increase prescription drug prices for Canadians.

Madam Speaker, I rise with respect to comments attributed to me in the Edmonton Journal of March 13, 1987, regarding the Deschenes Commission report.
I want to state that the intent of my remarks was to acknowledge that both Ukrainians and Jews had suffered enormous losses at the hands of oppressors.
In recognizing the tragic death of some 5.5 million Ukrainians, I in no way wished to minimize or downplay the atrocities and the evil of the Holocaust perpetrated by the Nazis.
If, inadvertently, my remarks have given offence or led anyone to believe I do not share a sense of outrage at the Holocaust, I categorically apologize and withdraw any statement, which may be interpreted as offensive to the Jewish community and indeed to any Canadian.

speakeroldname: Hon. William Rompkey (Grand Falls-White Bay- Labrador):
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I am pleased to have this opportunity to speak on one of the saddest pieces of legislation to come before us. It will do great damage to a very vulnerable sector of our society. It will impact mostly on the elderly, the sick and the disadvantaged. Why is this being done? We are told one reason is that more drug research will be done in Canada.
I want to address my remarks particularly to the amendment because it points out that there is no definition of research in the Bill. The Minister says he does not want to put a definition in the Bill for fear of limiting the kind of research to be done by a multinational. I want to remind him of the words of his Leader who said he was not afraid to impose prosperity on the regions. I say to him, do not be afraid to impose prosperity on the regions of this country. Do not limit
Patent Act
the amount of research because all over my riding holes are being dug in the ground in anticipation of the research centres which will be going up. There is a hole in Donovans Industrial Park in St. John's. I suspect the man digging that foundation is doing it in anticipation of the new research centre to go up there. In Wild Bight, White Bay, there is another hole in the ground and I suspect another research centre will be going up there in anticipation of this new legislation. We will probably see research centres growing up all over Newfoundland and Labrador. Indeed, research could become a new growth industry employing all those unemployed fishermen, all those miners laid off in Labrador City because of the downturn in the mining industry, and all those unemployed young people. No doubt they will get jobs in all those new research centres that are going to go up.
Well, that is a fiction. The record will show that R and D has not been done in Canada up until now and most certainly will not be done in the future because Canada has a small domestic market and historically the multinationals have chosen to perform R and D in their home country. I suspect that no matter what this legislation does that situation will continue. The multinationals will continue to do their research where they have done it before in spite of this legislation. I do not buy the argument that more research and development will come to Canada as a result of the passage of this Bill.
There is no question but that drug prices will rise. As a matter of fact, the Minister has admitted that, by passing along to the provinces $100 million over the next four years in anticipation that drug prices will rise so that the provinces will be able to fund, to a certain extent, the drug programs. However, that will be only a drop in the bucket. The real burden of the price increases which will come will be on the elderly, the sick, and particularly on low-income people.
A Bill on day care was introduced earlier this week. We are doing something about day care in this country because of the changes that are going on in Canadian society. There are more single-parent families today and most of the single parents are women who, of necessity, must look after their children somehow or other. They are doubly disadvantaged because, as we know, women are already in a disadvantaged position with regard to employment in this country. The average working woman is making 60 cents to every dollar earned by a man. I make that point because I believe we need to understand the changes which are going on in our society and understand the kind of people on whom this Bill will impact. The pressure will be exerted when children are sick and drugs have to be bought. That is when the unhappy effects will be felt.
The effects will also be felt by the elderly, the fastest growing section of the Canadian population. That range in our population will escalate dramatically during the next few years. We all know that as we age we have a greater dependency on medical help and drugs. I am starting to feel it

April 2, 1987
Patent Act
myself, although I am not that old. When drug prices increase the burden will be felt by the senior population as well.
These things will happen and that is why I think it is important to support the amendment before us today, and object to the measures in the Bill because there is no commitment to enforce the legislation. There is nothing built in which ensures that multinationals will live up to what they say they are going to do. I believe we would have been prepared to accept the reasonable position put forward by the Eastman report. Everyone understands that there must be some legitimate protection for people who invent new things, that there must be some legitimate compensation for them.
Elowever, legitimate and reasonable are the words upon which we must focus. I do not agree that we should say that they may design and introduce whatever new drugs they wish and can have a monopoly for a 10 year period. I do not know of anyone who willingly holds down prices in a monopoly. Unless there is some sort of competition, some balance in the market-place, people who have a monopoly on a product will charge as much as they can for it. That is part of the free market system. However, it seems to me that there is no reason the Government of Canada should hand such an opportunity to companies which are mostly American, while putting at a disadvantage distinctively Canadian companies which have grown up over the years.
There is no question that some price rise has to occur. The Eastman report suggested that a certain minimum price rise occur, that there be a royalty, and that possibly the period for the royalty might increase somewhat, but not to a 10 year period. In other words, the Government has gone well beyond what Eastman recommended. We will get not a reasonable increase for people who buy new drugs in the country, but a gouging of the Canadian consumer, particularly the elderly, those who are sick, and those who are on low incomes. That is the reality, Madam Speaker.
There are some people who say that there is really no difference between Parties anymore, that all people are Liberal-Conservatives, Conservative-Liberals, or whatever. However, it seems to me that this Bill puts into focus the difference in philosophy. When this Party was the Government it introduced, I believe in 1969, the regulations which have been in effect up until now through which there has been some competition in the market-place, which has kept the price of drugs down for Canadian consumers. There was something in the order of S200 million a year in savings to the Canadian people as a result of the legislation that was passed. Legislation has now been introduced which will dramatically drive up the price of drugs. That may not happen right away because this is a Sominex Bill, a sleeper Bill, but the price rises are coming.
When the Government tried to reduce old age pensions there was a mobilizing, for the first time, of gray power all across the country. This is the time for a re-enactment of that play, for the return of gray power. If we are going to do a job in this chamber of opposing this legislation I hope the seniors will once again come to the support of the Parties who are opposing
this, will mobilize their forces and tell the Government that they are not prepared to put up with legislation which impacts directly on them, by putting an undue and unfair burden on them over the next 10 years.

Madam Speaker, I would like to take this opportunity to say a few words about the amendment before the House which attempts to put into the Bill a definition of "research". Most of the Members of this House have at some time been in Opposition and have a healthy disrespect for Bills which leave too much to regulation. Any citizen who has dealt directly with the interpretation of legislation must have a concern with a Bill which leaves so much to regulation that in many cases the regulations become more important with regard to the impact of the Bill than the Bill itself.
Nothing is more central to this Bill than research, how it is defined and what research can be done in Canada. I understand that many of the people who appeared before the committee had concerns about this particular section and believed that research had to be much more clearly defined and detailed in the Bill. The clause in the Bill which says: "The Governor in Council may make regulations defining, for the purposes of this section, the expression 'research and development' ", leaves the matter up to Cabinet. It is our concern and that of the Official Opposition that this point should not be left to regulation.
The disadvantages of not adhering to this principle are pretty well known. When precise instructions are not in legislation it is left to a regulator and there is always a possibility that the regulator will interpret the Act in a way quite different than what was originally intended when Parliament passed the Act. We are not satisfied to leave the definition of "research" to the Cabinet. We believe the Cabinet has already caved in to the multinational companies and, with the establishment of regulations, will continue to cave in.
One of the great disadvantages of leaving the definition to the regulators is that it is a hidden process. It does not provide for input from a large number of people. The legislative structure of the Bill allows all of us to talk about it. It allows hearings and discussion, but that does not happen in the making of regulations. A regulation can be changed very quickly, for example, by another regulation. Even if we now receive regulations from the Government under this Act, that would not make us feel secure that the definition would be the same next year because those regulations can be replaced by other regulations.
Often this process of changing a regulation or replacing a regulation goes unnoticed, yet it can have enormous implications. We have found in the past that regulations often allow the vested interests of those who have the time and money, and the reason, to impact on the Cabinet. The changing of
April 2, 1987

regulations is often controlled by that particular group. That is not in the public interest, or in the interests of Parliament.
The Hon. Member for Cape Breton-East Richmond (Mr. Dingwall) has made a commendable attempt to present a statutory definition of "research". The Hon. Member for Winnipeg North (Mr. Orlikow) has also made an attempt to put into this Act a definition of "research" which would force the people who are going to be governed by this Bill to recognize that they have a greater responsibility.
Some kind of amendment to the R and D definition is needed. People who appeared before the committee toid us that it is now a kind of logical decision. We have no guarantees that the companies will invest the sums they say they are committed to. We have no guarantees that the investments will be in research rather than in any other kind of investment. We have no guarantees that the investment will be in research or even in basic research of useful medicines. The investment may instead be in processes and other things which really have nothing to do with the basic idea of research into pharmaceuticals.
What we do have is some indication of how the companies intend to proceed toward meeting their goals. As the Minister for Consumer and Corporate Affairs (Mr. Andre) has expressed it, there will be 3,000 high-quality jobs created for Canadian scientists and biochemists over the next 10 years. The Minister made that statement in his attempts to justify this Bill. The access to information application made by Southam News indicates that the Minister, even as he made this statement, did not believe it. What that document shows is that of the 3,000 jobs, there will be 1,148 employed by the industry in professional categories. So the statement of 3,000 jobs for highly-qualified people has become 1,148 in the professional category. There will be another 541 persons employed extramurally, probably in universities and research institutes. There are 652 jobs classified as "technical", which means lab technicians who would have an undergraduate or community college standing. There are 620 "others" who turn out to be, in the words of the Department of Consumer and Corporate Affairs, managers, cleaners, animal keepers, statisticians and clerks. These are not what we would consider highly qualified scientists and biochemists. These jobs are almost menial in their level. Are these the kind of jobs to which we are committing a large amount of money?
What we have seen in the context of this particular Bill, as far as the Government is concerned, is that very little will be delivered for what it will cost all Canadians in terms of increased drug costs. The reluctance of the Government to accept the definition of "research" shows it is really in the pockets of the multinationals. The multinationals do not want to be confined and committed to a long-term investment in research in Canada.

Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to be able to rise today to address Bill C-22, specifically the amendment setting forth the definition of "research"
Patent Act
proposed by a representative of the Liberal Party. In doing so,
I am a little sorry there are not more Members of the Liberal Party in the House to hear me, because I intend to start by praising the Liberal Party for its political courage in attempting to define "research". That political courage means more when we consider that it was the Liberal Government, after all, which brought in the Scientific Research Tax Credit which cost the taxpayers something in the region of $3 billion. I think it shows that in the development of a political party there are times when the great tragedies and failures that political party has inflicted on the country in the past must in a sense be set aside in the search for better legislative solutions in the future. Therefore, I see this as very much being an acknowledgement by the Liberal Party of how much it has cost this country in the past in not properly defining and limiting the eligibility of research expenditures for tax credit treatment.
I must say that, having grasped that particular nettle and acknowledged the grave derelictions in Liberal history, that Party has not come up with what I would accept as the best offer of a definition of "research". I will talk later about why that definition of research is so important to this Bill. It has come up with what I believe is a somewhat incomplete definition. I must say that even were there no partisan considerations involved, and of course there are, I would prefer the definition that has been put forward in Motion No. 43 by my very distinguished and erudite colleague, the Hon. Member for Winnipeg North (Mr. Orlikow), who, as I am sure every Member of this House is aware, has worked on this sort of problem and this sort of legislative project for very many years in the House. He has built up an enormous understanding of the significance of proper definition to the ultimate effectiveness of a Bill.
After all, what Bill C-22 aims to do, essentially, is open the floodgates to profiteering on the part of multinational drug companies. It aims to open them in such a way that the multinationals will not have to look at possible legislative differences between Canada and the United States when they are pushing a drug development project. In saying this I am not taking away from the significance, the relevance or, indeed, the hope for the future that some of these prescription medication development projects entail. I think we are well aware that, but for the progress that has been made over the past century in the development of medication, the public health scenario in North America and, indeed, in the world would be much bleaker than it is today.
But the existence of a system which sometimes produces excellent results and sometimes satisfactory results is no excuse for failing to attempt to develop or, indeed, in this case maintain a superior system. After all, resources are the common currency. Financial resources are the very language of government. The devotion of an excessive proportion of resources, as would be the case in the sort of profit-oriented regime proposed by the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs (Mr. Andre), to the rewarding through the profit

April 2, 1987
Patent Act
mechanism of the multinational drug companies is not in the best interests of an intelligent allocation of resources or in the best interests of Canadian health care consumers.
What was wrong with the system that we had before the Government introduced its proposed amendments to the Patent Act as set out in Bill C-22? That system did not appear to deny Canadians access to new medication technology or to new medications. It could never have been said about that system that it crippled any of the multinational drug companies. It could never have been said that it drove them out of business. I do not think that it could ever have been said that under the present regime of patent protection the opportunities for drug companies to recoup their research were limited or in any way impaired below a reasonable expectation of return and a reasonable flow of funds for the development of future research. In going beyond the Eastman report in Bill C-22 the Government has essentially made a preliminary concession to the United States in terms of the trade negotiations. I am concerned about the status of these preliminary concessions because it seems to me that Canada is giving preliminary concessions in more than one negotiation in order to bring the other side to the table in a good mood. I do not think that is an appropriate basis on which to conduct bilateral trade negotiations. I do not think that it is an appropriate basis on which to negotiate the allocation of cod stocks on the Grand Banks of Newfoundland. I do not think that it is an appropriate basis on which to go into multilateral trade negotiations, for example. But, indeed, this might become the expectation of those who go into negotiations with the Canadian Government, if a pattern is set, providing these preliminary sweeteners bring the other parties to the negotiation table.
My colleague, the Hon. Member for Prince Albert (Mr. Hovdebo), provided a very detailed and, I believe, a very precise analysis of just what the 3,000 so-called high technology research jobs that the Government is claiming come down to. I think it is worthwhile to put on the record again that this is essentially a chimera, that there are no guarantees attached to those 3,000 supposed jobs. The Government really does not have any worthwhile assurances that those jobs will in fact be created.
It is also worthwhile to remind the Government that the Canadian system of drug licensing and the Canadian regulations, with their lower limits on patent protection, are indeed something that have been the subject of study. I believe it was a U.S. Congressional committee which rather liked the Canadian example and felt that it lay within its responsibility-indeed it was its duty as legislators of our great neighbour to the south-to examine the Canadian system to determine whether or not it might be applicable to the United States.
I would like to point out also that the delayed effect essentially allows the Government to forever slide out of any analysis or any form of objective assessment of any benefits that may be realized under Bill C-22. We may expect that Motions Nos. 2 and 43 will be rejected by the House, since the Government will exercise its majority. However, without the
inclusion of one or other of these motions there will not be an opportunity for the Government and for the public of Canada to assess in some objective way if this Bill has achieved its objectives.
On the contrary, the Government wishes to proceed by regulation which, of course, is a hidden process. It wants to go by regulation since regulations can be changed virtually at will and virtually without any reference to Parliament or the public. It wants to go with regulation because that will allow the continuance of that obviously cozy, obviously mutually rewarding relationship which the Government has established with those same multinational drug companies. We know that in the case of powerful and committed lobbies, such as those of the multinational drug companies, regulations are at the mercy of those interests. Unfortunately, the natural order of things appears to be that regulations are involved to accommodate the industry and its appetite for profit and not to regulate it in the best interests of Canadians.

Madam Speaker, I am pleased to be able to participate in the debate on this important amendment which would ensure that there is a definition of research in Bill C-22. My colleague, the Hon. Member for Winnipeg North (Mr. Orlikow), who has done an outstanding job on behalf of New Democrats all across Canada-indeed on behalf of the people of Canada-with respect to this legislation has proposed an alternate definition which, quite frankly, is more tightly drafted and is in fact preferable to the proposal of my colleague, the Hon. Member for Cape Breton-East Richmond (Mr. Dingwall), although I am certainly pleased to support his proposal as well.
The nub of this issue is the extent to which we as Members of Parliament are prepared to leave to Cabinet the definition of "research". I believe it is essential for us, as elected representatives of the people, as parliamentarians, to define this fundamental concept in the legislation. The whole thrust of the Government's amendment is that there will be a major expansion of jobs in the research sector in Canada if this legislation is adopted. The Government admits, as it has to, that the cost of drugs in Canada will increase, and in some cases increase dramatically, as a result of the passage of this legislation; but it says that it is prepared to accept those increases in the prices of drugs because, in exchange, it is going to create a lot of new jobs in Canada in the area of research and development.
Not true.

Madam Speaker, I think we have to examine very carefully whether this basic foundation for the Government's legislation is well founded. We have to ask ourselves, for example, whether the jobs to be created in research and development will be jobs created in the area of basic research, or whether they will be jobs created in the area of clinical research. I suspect, Madam Speaker, as witness after witness
April 2, 1987

who appeared before the legislative committee on this Bill confirmed, they will not be primarily in the area of basic research at all; that they will be, overwhelmingly, in the area of clinical research.
As well, Madam Speaker, it is important that we underline the fact that the promise of additional jobs in the pharmaceutical industry is not one that is directly based solely on the passage of this legislation. We have to recognize that in Canada we have an aging population, and as the population ages the demand for pharmaceutical drugs increases. So, the projection of new jobs in Canada is not only as a result of the adoption of this legislation, to which only a small part would be attributable, but also, to a very significant extent, to the natural increase in the demand for drugs on the part of an aging population.
Madam Speaker, my constituents in Burnaby have asked me why it is that the Government is determined to proceed with a measure which is going to result in significantly increased prices for new drugs for the elderly, for the sick, for the disabled. As well, Madam Speaker, it is a measure which will result in an over-all increase in taxes in those provinces which have pharmacare plans.
I have been asked what is the basis for this. A senior citizen in the New Vista highrise in Burnaby asked me why it is that the Government is so determined to increase drug prices, what is the advantage of this, and whether it is going to create new jobs. One of the seniors said that she had received a letter from the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs (Mr. Andre) in which the Minister had promised that there would be a minimum of 3,000 high quality jobs for Canadian scientists and biochemists created over the next 10 years. She said to me: "I have a grandson who is studying chemistry at university, and we are concerned that there aren't enough jobs for young scientists in Canada. So obviously, if there is a real possibility of a significant expansion of jobs in basic research in Canada, that is something that all of us would welcome".
But, Madam Speaker, when one reads between the lines, as my colleagues have already noted, one finds that the promise of 3,000 high quality jobs for Canadian scientists and biochemists is a myth, is a fabrication. It is just not going to happen. The Government's own documents show that these so-called 3,000 jobs will not be jobs in the professional categories, let alone in basic research; rather, a significant number of those people will in fact be employed, to use the words of the Department of Consumer and Corporate Affairs, "as managers, cleaners, animal keepers, statisticians, and clerks".
No PhDs.

Madam Speaker, the reality in Canada today is that some of our cleaners and some of our clerks are in fact PhDs, are people who, while highly trained, cannot find employment in their fields. As a result of the failure of this Government's policy, and the failure of the policies of the Government before it, many of these people are driving taxis or are in fact working as clerks or as animal keepers.
Patent Act
We in the New Democratic Party, Madam Speaker, believe that we should be using the resources of the people of Canada. We believe that we should be challenging our young people; that we should be encouraging them to engage in basic research-but not, Madam Speaker, in the way that the Government has proposed.
My colleague from Windsor-Walkerville (Mr. McCurdy) has spoken, often eloquently, on the subject of the crisis in funding for post-secondary education in Canada. Instead of pouring hundreds of millions of dollars into the coffers of multinational drug companies, why not put money into the future of the young people of this country by strengthening the system of post-secondary education in Canada?
When my constituents in Burnaby, Madam Speaker, asked me why it is that the Government wants to hit the old, why it is that they want to hit the sick, the disabled, I had a look at the Government's political agenda, and, Madam Speaker, what I found was very interesting. I found that part and parcel of the free trade negotiations between Canada and the United States is a commitment by the Progressive Conservative Government and the Prime Minister of Canada (Mr. Mulroney) to the multinational drug companies in the United States that their concerns will be taken care of. That is the deal; that is the fix, Madam Speaker.
Clayton Yeutter, the chief U.S. negotiator on free trade, in a speech delivered in Chicago in October of last year, made the following statement:
We have longstanding concerns regarding the inadequate protection in Canada
of pharmaceutical patents, as well as the absence of copyright protection of
U.S. broadcasting which is picked up and retransmitted throughout Canada.
We wish to secure adequate intellectual property protection in both of these
areas.
So, what we see here, Madam Speaker, is an attempt to placate American national drug companies. And who is being sacrificed? It is those who are most vulnerable in Canada today: the elderly, the sick, the disabled. And it is the poor, Madam Speaker, whose taxes will increase with the increase in the cost of provincial pharmacare plans.
Recently, Madam Speaker, we saw a budget tabled in the Province of British Columbia which will result in a significant increase in the cost of drugs right away to the elderly, an increase of some $250 a year-and this to those who can least afford to pay. That increase comes as a result of the Vander Zalm Government proposal to add on the increased costs to the B.C. pharmacare plan.
The senior citizens of Canada, Madam Speaker, have spoken out strongly, and unanimously against this Government's proposal to destroy what is an effective plan to keep the price of pharmaceutical drugs in Canada down. My colleague, the Member for Nickel Belt (Mr. Rodriguez) is in the Chamber. He spoke yesterday with fire and brimstone-
And eloquence.

-about the history of this matter. I do not think I have to remind Canadians, Madam Speaker, that it

April 2, 1987
Patent Act
was the previous Liberal Government which first set out to erode the protections in this area; that it was the then Liberal Government, Madam Speaker, that appointed Martin O'Connell to head a commission on the subject, an individual who in fact was buddy-buddy with the multinational drug companies. Canadians know that history, Madam Speaker. They are well aware of the fact that this is a process which was started by the Liberals and which is now being continued by the Conservatives. The only Party which has consistently spoken out in favour of the interests of Canadian consumers, the elderly, the poor, the disabled in Canada, is the New Democratic Party, and we will continue to speak out on their behalf.
You are signalling me, Madam Speaker, that my time is in fact coming to an end on this particular amendment.
With regret.

Obviously, my colleagues will be continuing, during the course of the next weeks and months, to speak out on this important Bill. 1 want to assure, Madam Speaker, not only the people of Burnaby but all of the people of this country, that there is one Party which is consistent in its determination to keep the cost of pharmaceutical drugs down, to enhance the quality of research in Canada, to provide jobs for young Canadian scientists, and that Party, Madam Speaker, is the New Democratic Party of Canada.
Hear, hear!

He said: Madam Speaker, as a result of a ruling by the Speaker, Motions Nos. 3, 4, 5, 11, 13, and 15 have been grouped for the purposes of debate, but I believe they have been split for the purposes of a vote which will take place at a later time.
April 2, 1987

With regard to Motions Nos. 3, 13, and 15, they will delete product patents from the legislation, which is the purpose of the amendment. As the law now stands, only process patents can be granted. Bill C-22 would allow product patents to be granted as well. Canadian biotechnology firms say that this change will effectively put them out of business.
I thought it was the intention of the Government of the day to try to foster new economic activity in the country, not to retard or negative in any way those industries already in place. However, with the way in which Bill C-22 is drafted, it will have the opposite effect of the stated intention of the Government. Biotechnology firms want to keep the process of genetic engineering patentable, but because these substances are naturally occurring they do not believe that the product developed from the use of process should be patentable.
For example, companies like Cangene, which appeared before the legislative committee on Bill C-22, made a very forceful, thoughtful, and reasonable presentation. Cangene extracts naturally occurring substances, genes, from healthy individuals and injects them into unhealthy individuals in a manner which triggers the unhealthy individual to manufacture the substance in his or her own body. The way the Bill now stands, it would prevent companies like Cangene, which are very actively involved in the biotechnology sector of the pharmaceutical industry or the health science industry, from carrying on their activities in a viable way.
As we debate the provisions of Bill C-22, I think it is important to try to maintain a clear and unequivocal objective. It is the stated intention, desire, and objective of our Party that we have a balanced approach to the vital elements which make up the pharmaceutical industry in Canada. Whether one looks at it from the point of view of the creation of new jobs, from the aspect of research and development and what will take place in Canada as a result of Bill C-22 being passed into law, or from the perspective of Canadian consumers who must purchase prescription drugs, it is clear that Bill C-22 will not allow us to attain that particular objective.
The Government is discriminating or unwisely prohibiting certain firms in that sector from prospering. We think that is wrong, Madam Speaker. If one has to have a Canadian pharmaceutical industry, one has to bring in public policy which addresses all of the concerns to achieve that result. Unfortunately, and I say this with great sincerity, Bill C-22 has major omissions regarding that objective.
Motions Nos. 4, 5 and 11, and I say this as simply as I can, Madam Speaker, because I know you are very attentive to these various amendments, deal with the recommendations contained in Dr. Harry Eastman's report. That report was commissioned by the previous administration whereby Dr. Eastman studied the subject at great length. It would be fair to say that from all perspectives he is indeed an authority on the pharmaceutical industry. Motions Nos. 4, 5 and 11, deal with Dr. Eastman's recommendations, namely, a four-year period of
Patent Act
exclusivity after the granting of a notice of compliance. Here is where one will probably want to talk about Dr. Eastman's recommendations regarding the pharmaceutical royalty fund. I know members opposite, particularly those who served on the legislative committee, had some difficulties grasping-I do not say this to be disputatious or to be mean-and comprehending the thrusts of Dr. Eastman's recommendations regarding that. In summary, companies would pay into the pharmaceutical royalty fund and would receive back a proportion in accordance with the amount of research and development they conduct here in Canada. Dr. Eastman has felt that by increasing royalties rather than unduly-this is very key- lengthening patent protection we would avoid the anticompetitive aspect of exclusivity.
Since the Chair has ruled that these motions have been grouped together for the purposes of debate, let me conclude in the few minutes I have by saying that the present amendment of the administration of the Conservative Government grants an extended monopoly provision to multinational companies in this country. One is concerned with trying to develop and enhance the Canadian pharmaceutical industry but the Bill has grave and serious omissions with other elements regarding consumers, research and development. It is acknowledging in Bill C-22 that the concept of intellectual property ought to be the main thrust of a possible tool, as I believe Bill C-22 could be, for economic development in Canada.
My Party has accepted the recommendations of Dr. Eastman because he is an authority and because he has studied the subject. We believe the recommendations to be reasonable. Having said all of that, I have to clearly and unequivocally dissociate myself from what the Government is attempting to do. I disagree with its extended monopoly provisions to brand name companies. Nothing has been done about prices other than to pay lip service. In paying lip service, they have acknowledged, quite rightly, that prices in Canada will rise by an exorbitant amount. They have done nothing in terms of clear enforceable guarantees, vis-a-vis commitments for research and development.
Bill C-22 has major omissions. We as a Party disagree with the thrust of Bill C-22. We have submitted these amendments to try to improve upon the Bill. I would hope that the Government would accept our amendments because they are both reasonable and, I think, address all of the vital elements that go into developing a Canadian pharmaceutical industry.
The committee has heard a number of witnesses from all walks of life who are opposed to the Government's desire and intention to give unfettered monopoly sanctions or provisions to the multinational corporations. The amendments we are putting forward today, and 1 know my colleague from the New Democratic Party has an amendment and will probably want to speak to that directly himself, are trying to address a very important element of the Canadian economy.

Madam Speaker, I rise to support the thrust of these amendments, one of which,

April 2, 1987
Patent Act
Motion No. 4,1 moved on behalf of our Party. We should keep in mind the history of this Bill. Without going into a lengthy historical account, let me remind Hon. Members and the Minister that until 1969 our system of legislation for patent protection of prescription drugs was very much like the system in the United States. As a result we had the second highest prescription drug prices in the world.
A whole series of inquiries were held by the Restrictive Trade Practices Commission, eventually by a parliamentary committee headed by a member at that time, Dr. Harley, and it was substantiated very clearly that Canadians were paying far too much for prescription drugs.
In 1969 the legislation was changed. After companies had satisfied health authorities that a drug would be medically safe and adequate they could get a licence to produce the drug. This drug had already been researched and developed by another company, usually a multinational, and companies we call generic companies could produce that same drug after paying a royalty fee to the original company.
After 1969, as a result of that change in the legislation, prices for prescription drugs in Canada have been among the lowest of the industrialized countries. The multinational corporations were, to say the least, unhappy about this and they began very quickly to mount a campaign against it. They are very powerful politically. They have a lot of money to help political Parties, Members of Parliament or candidates who want to become Members of Parliament with campaign funds. Their parent companies which are usually in the United States have tremendous power in the United States.
The multinationals were not simply worried about what had happened in Canada, they were worried that the American public would see the success of the program we instituted in Canada and would begin to call for a similar program in the United States. That in fact happened. Congressman Waxman heads up of a subcommittee which has studied this question extensively. He is moving to bring in the kind of program we have had in Canada since 1969. Governor Cuomo of New York State has found that the state is facing increasing costs because senior citizens who qualify for Medicaid and Medicare programs in that state receive all or part of their prescription costs from the state. The state is looking at these escalating costs and is now taking steps to encourage pharmacists to use generic drugs when filling prescriptions for senior citizens.
The then Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs in the Liberal Government, the Hon. Member for Papineau (Mr. Ouellet), listened to the complaints of the multinational companies and wanted to do something about them. However, he realized that there would be a great deal of pressure in opposition to any major change so he appointed a professor from the University of Toronto, Professor Eastman, to study the problem. Professor Eastman conducted a very lengthy study, but by the time he brought his report to Parliament the
election had taken place and we had a new Government, a Conservative Government, but not a very progressive one.
What happened to Professor Eastman's report? Did the Government greet it with interest and hope? No, it virtually hid the report. The Government which talks so much about being open and wanting to listen to people then proceeded to try to achieve for the multinational corporations what they wanted, and that was a much longer period of exclusivity after having developed new drugs so that they could set prices at the levels they wanted. The Government proceeded to try to get for the multinational pharmaceutical companies what they wanted by arranging for secret meetings to be held between the members of the Pharmaceutical Manufacturers Association of Canada, representatives from the multinationals and representatives from the generic companies. The Government was telling the generic companies that they had better agree to something and give something up or else the Government would bring in legislation which they would like even less. There was very little talk about Professor Eastman's report or its merits.
When the many organizations that represent the people of Canada realized what was happening, they began to express their opposition to it. The Consumers' Association of Canada is not a very radical organization. It is an organization that is very cautious and careful. It very carefully examines issues which are of concern to consumers before it comes to a conclusion. As soon as that organization looked at the Bill which was brought in by the former Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs, it made it very clear that it was very critical of the Bill and it has continued to oppose it. The Canadian Labour Congress and unions associated with it, seniors' organizations almost without exception and farm groups such as Keystone Agricultural Producers all opposed the Bill virtually from the day it came out.
Then began the waffling. We now have a Bill before us which supposedly implements the proposals of Professor Eastman's report. If one were to examine the Bill and compare it with Professor Eastman's proposals, one would see that they have very little in common.
The Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs (Mr. Andre) has said repeatedly that, as a result of this Bill, the cost of prescription drugs will not rise or at least not for some considerable time. Professor Eastman on the other hand made it very clear, both in his report and in his testimony before the committee, that evidence showed that the cost of prescription drugs would go up and quite substantially. In testimony before the committee, he pointed out that as a result of this Bill, pharmaceutical companies would have an extra six years of exclusivity during which they could set prices.
Let me conclude by saying to the Minister that there is evidence before us now that the cost will rise. A few days ago, the Social Credit Government of British Columbia presented a Budget. In it the cost of prescription drugs that will be borne by a family in British Columbia, before the Government plan picks up the rest, has been increased to $250 per family. This
April 2, 1987

Bill is deficient. The amendment I moved and the amendment moved by the representative of the Liberal Party should be supported.

Madam Speaker, I rise to speak to the motion put forward by my colleague, the Hon. Member for Cape Breton-East Richmond (Mr. Dingwall), and Motion No. 4 put forward by the Hon. Member for Winnipeg North (Mr. Orlikow). My constituents and the people of Prince Edward Island are very concerned about this Bill. Since this Bill was brought forward by the Government I have received, on a daily basis, letters and cards from my constituents protesting it. I have also received numerous phone calls in both my riding office and my Ottawa office. My office assistant tells me that at least 10 to 15 calls a day come in regarding Bill C-22 which the Government is ramming through this House.
These cards I have here inform me of the strong objection these individuals have to the proposed regressive changes to the Patent Act. They request me, as their Member of Parliament, to do everything in my power to see that this proposed rip-off of Canadians through exorbitant increases in drug prices is not allowed to pass. Among those who have sent me cards are Clifford Arsenault, Ferdinand Gallant, Michael Gaudet, Corinne Kay, Sidney Richards, James Fraser, Mitchell Kahili, James Douglas, Anthony Perry, Cindy Douglas, Earl Matthews, and Stewart McKenna. These people are from Ellerslie, Elmsdale, Summerside, St. Nicholas, Miscouche and Wellington, Prince Edward Island. They are all ordinary, hard-working Canadians with families. They are finding it extremely difficult to get along on the wages they are able to bring home. In times like this we see that tax increases on one thing and another are eroding the little bit of disposable income these people have. It is almost a disaster. It has gotten to the point where they can no longer afford any increases whatsoever in taxes or anything else. This Bill is a form of indirect tax and it is not needed. There is no need for the Government to change the Patent Act in order to allow the multinational drug companies to increase their profits.
The other day I referred to a letter that was sent to the Minister by Mr. Robert Wygant, a man who spent 25 years in the pharmaceutical industry in Canada. I read the letter into the record for a good reason. It was one of the best and clearest letters that I have ever received from a constituent on this subject. The man pointed out quite clearly the profits the drug companies are making. He also pointed out that it is wrong to think very much research is going to be carried out in this country when something less than 5 per cent of total research is done in the U.S. where they have patent legislation which prohibits these sorts of profits.
I have eight Royal Canadian Legion branches in my riding representing thousands of veterans. We all know those living on veterans' pensions are not living high on the hog. Those people are concerned about this legislation and I want to give

this House the thinking of one branch of the Royal Canadian Legion. The branch is not in my riding, but in the riding of the Hon. Member for Malpeque (Mr. Gass). The branch sent me a copy of the letter. The letter says:
The members of North Rustico Legion Branch 13 by a motion with 100 per

We are 100 per cent against the Federal Government's introduction of a bill to

Since becoming a Member of Parliament in 1980, I have never seen such a hue and cry, such outrage as I have now except perhaps when the Government tried to deindex old age pensions.
The legislature of Prince Edward Island unanimously approved a resolution condemning the Government and asking it to withdraw this legislation. I have talked at length with the Minister for Health and Social Services of Prince Edward Island, the Hon. Keith Milligan, and he wrote the federal Minister and made numerous overtures to the Government asking it to withdraw this legislation. It is not just the Government of the day in that province, which happens to be a Liberal Government, that is protesting. The Government of former Premier James Lee also made approaches to the federal Government asking it to withdraw this Bill and avoid increasing drug prices for Canadians.
Statistics point out quite clearly that Prince Edward Island has the highest percentage of elderly people per capita in Canada. I do not know whether that is because of the fresh air or the beautiful surroundings, but people live longer there, and there are statistics to prove it. We all know that there is more sickness and more need on the part of senior citizens to depend on prescription drugs. Those are the people who will be the hardest hit by this legislation. This legislation irks them, and it irks me as their representative. I speak out on their behalf, unlike the other three Members from Prince Edward Island. I have not heard them say one word on this Bill. Obviously they are following along the Government road of ramming this legislation through. They may not admit it, but at some time or other they have been told to follow the Government's lead. They have been told that some research will come to the Province of Prince Edward Island at the University of P.E.I. As they say in Prince Edward Island, that just ain't so. There will be no research at the University of Prince Edward Island because we do not have a medical component there. As I said before, this is a totally misleading statement because we have heard experts in the field say that of the total research that is now done on new drugs less than 5 per cent is done in Canada or the United States and there is legislation already in place in the United States which would prohibit this sort of research being done.
