subsubtopic: ACID RAIN-PRIME MINISTER'S FORTHCOMING MEETING WITH UNITED STATES PRESIDENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, Canadians are beginning to wonder about the acid rain strategy of the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney). His acceptance of research and demonstration as progress means that Canada is being sidetracked on acid rain cuts. Unfortunately, the debate is now on how much money should be spent, over how many years, for research and demonstration, instead of pollution cuts.
On the eve of the third summit, Canadians expect their Prime Minister to speak frankly and ask that the dumping of acid rain pollution into Canada be stopped. We urge the Prime Minister to put before the President next Sunday a blueprint for cutting acid rain crossing into Canada, including quantities, targets, and deadlines. We must protect the Canadian environment. Canada must spell out what Canadians want. The Prime Minister's acid rain strategy must reassure, not create doubts, in the minds of Canadians.

subtopic: SUGAR BEET STABILIZATION PLAN-NON-PARTICIPATION BY MANITOBA
SUGAR BEET STABILIZATION PLAN-NON-PARTICIPATION BY MANITOBA
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am pleased the federal Government has announced it will sign a tripartite stabilization plan for sugar beets with the producers and the provincial Government of Alberta. Unfortunately, even though Manitoba's Minister of Agriculture is a signatory to the national agriculture strategy, which recognizes that both levels of government have a responsibility to support agriculture, the Province of Manitoba is unwilling to make a commitment to this plan.
Tripartite stabilization agreements prove that the two levels of government and producers can work together to support agriculture. The tripartite stabilization plan for hogs, in which Manitoba does participate, is a good example of how productive that co-operation can be.
The federal Government, the provincial Government of Alberta and producers in both Alberta and Manitoba all support the concept of the proposed tripartite stabilization plan. These parties believe in the future of the sugar beet industry and are willing to commit to it. I hope we will soon see the same sort of commitment from the Province of Manitoba.

Mr. Speaker, early this week the Government received a lot of advice on how to solve Canada's child care crisis. The common claim running through all proposals is that it provide child care choices to parents. Three key elements allow parents to choose child care uniquely suited to their family's needs. First, those child care arrangements must exist from which to choose. Second, the child care arrangements must be affordable to the family. Most important of all, child care arrangements must ensure quality care for children.
Canadians know these three elements cannot be achieved through Conservative tax credits which do not even cover the cost of care, and a laissez-faire free market attitude to child care. Canadians will reject the Liberal philosophy which sees child care as an extension of the welfare system. Canadians overwhelmingly told the Special Committee on Child Care that they want a publicly financed system developed at the community level with parent input, non-profit and accountable, with quality controls.
It is not too late for the Government to get a copy of the New Democratic Party's proposals entitled "Caring for Canada's Children".
April 2, 1987

subtopic: EXPRESSION OF SYMPATHY FOR VICTIMS OF ACCIDENT AT GASPE COPPER MINE AT MURDOCHVILLE
EXPRESSION OF SYMPATHY FOR VICTIMS OF ACCIDENT AT GASPE COPPER MINE AT MURDOCHVILLE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, once again disaster has struck in the riding of Gaspe.
Last night, there was an accident at the copper mine in Murdochville in the Gaspe. Later that night, 56 miners were still trapped in the tunnels of the Gaspe Copper Mine.
At two o'clock this afternoon, we have had some relatively reassuring news about 33 miners with whom the rescue team is in constant communication, but we also know that 17 workers have not yet been reached. Six were able to get out of the mine, one of whom was taken to hospital and one, unfortunately, is dead.
Mr. Speaker, the House will recall that on October 19 last year, three young mothers and three children lost their lives as a result of an explosion in a pharmacy at Sainte-Anne-des-Monts.
Mr. Speaker, in a region like mine that already has so many social and economic problems, the impact of a tragedy like this one goes beyond the immediate family to affect every Gaspe-sian, both in the Gaspe and outside, as well as former and present miners across this country.
Mr. Speaker, I am sure that you yourself and Hon. Members will join me in expressing our constant support for the miners, their families and the management of Gaspe Copper.

Mr. Speaker, the Tory Government has abandoned tens of thousands of farmers when they are facing the worst debt crisis since the 1930s. Fully 30 per cent of Canadian farmers now face insolvency or serious financial difficulty. Last week the Agriculture Committee heard tobacco farmers who had been promised action to help them to adjust to declining markets, prices and land values, blast the Government for its lack of action. The Tories had promised these farmers five cents from the 25 cent-per-pack tax imposed by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) in May of 1985 in an assistance program. That promise has not been kept, yet, daily, farmers are being forced off the land and a terrible personal toll is being taken.
These farmers were also promised a national marketing board by the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney). However, twoand-a-half years have passed and still no national marketing board has been established.
I call on the Government to keep its promise to these desperate farmers facing the loss of their farms, their livelihoods, and their homes.

subtopic: ACID RAIN-NEW BRUNSWICK'S WILLINGNESS TO SIGN AGREEMENT
ACID RAIN-NEW BRUNSWICK'S WILLINGNESS TO SIGN AGREEMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this morning at a meeting of the Acid Rain Committee, Premier Richard Hatfield advised that through negotiation with the federal Minister of the Environment (Mr. McMillan) he has reached the point at which he will recommend to the Government of New Brunswick that an agreement on the control of acid rain be signed. The Premier pointed out to the committee that New Brunswick has led the way in its sensitivity on environmental matters and has met its 1994 commitment of 185,000 tonnes of S02 many months ago.
The Premier assured the committee and the nation that New Brunswick's willingness to sign the agreement is consistent with its track record on pollution control and emphasizes the fact that the province has done, is doing, and will continue to do all that is necessary to carry its fair share and more to address this critical issue.

subtopic: REPAYMENT OF HIGH INTEREST RATE LOANS
REPAYMENT OF HIGH INTEREST RATE LOANS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, a Government which has admitted the need for action to reduce interest rates on credit cards should take note of another interest rate problem-the exorbitant rates charged students under the Canada Student Loan Plan. Students are still paying off loans at high rates of interest on loans taken out when the rates were higher. Some 200,000 students are paying rates of 16 per cent.
The high rates of interest are only part of the problem of the high debt load students are forced to assume. Some months ago now I took a number of particular horror stories to the Minister for action. He agreed that procedures needed to be improved in order to prevent such cases from recurring. So far nothing has been done.
Student leaders across the country agree that we need a national grant scheme, not just loans. Presumably this will be discussed at the forum on post-secondary education when it is held in the fall. In the meantime, the Secretary of State (Mr. Crombie) should move to correct the deficiencies of the

April 2, 1987
present system. He should take immediate action toward the reduction of those interest rates. Students should not have to start their working lives with such crippling debts. Our students deserve a better break, and the federal Government has its role with the provinces in providing it.

Mr. Speaker, my constituency of Sarnia-Lambton is known across the country and, indeed, throughout the world, as the chemical valley of Canada. The Canadian industry located there works tirelessly to remain competitive and productive in today's rapidly changing technological market. For this reason our Prime Minister's (Mr. Mulroney) decision to establish and chair the National Advisory Board for Science and Technology is applauded by this industry in Sarnia-Lambton.
A locally based multinational company in my community, Polysar Limited, is the world's largest producer of synthetic latex and rubber. Polysar is one of Canada's largest exporters of manufactured goods and last year accomplished $1.8 billion in sales overseas.
To maintain its position Polysar is heavily involved in R and D. Its current research efforts rank Polysar in the top 15 of all corporations doing research in Canada. Last year over $40 million was invested by Polysar in research and development. As a result Polysar is about to introduce to the world a new product developed in its Sarnia R and D laboratories.
Canada's future rests in the advancement of science and technology. I join with local industry in congratulating our Prime Minister on his recognition of the important field of R and D.

Mr. Speaker, most Canadians know that our farmers have been suffering from low commodity prices, whether it be with respect to grain, potatoes, or beef, just to name a few. Our farmers need all the help they can get, and the Farm Credit Corporation has to do its part.
I want to bring to the attention of the House the excessive lending rates charged by the Farm Credit Corporation. Its interest rate on five-year loans is 10.75 per cent, and for loans with terms over five years the rate is 11 per cent. At the same time chartered banks charge our farmers about prime plus 1
per cent, or 9.75 per cent. Farmers in my constituency believe that this is unfair, and I share their view.
This is the planting season, and farmers need financial assistance from the Farm Credit Corporation. I urge the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Wise) to intervene and instruct the Farm Credit Corporation to give our farmers a break.
Hear, hear!

speakeroldname: Right Hon. John N. Turner (Leader of the Opposition):

Mr. Speaker, 48 per cent of single people under the age of 25 in Canada live below the poverty line; 100,000 young people with children also live below the poverty line.

Shame!

maintopic: CANADA-UNITED STATES NEGOTIATIONS-IMPORTANCE TO WORKERS IN CHURCHILL RIDING
CANADA-UNITED STATES NEGOTIATIONS-IMPORTANCE TO WORKERS IN CHURCHILL RIDING
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the opposition of the NDP and the Member for Churchill (Mr. Murphy) to the Canada-U.S. trade negotiations is putting jobs in peril in that Member's own riding in northern Manitoba.
Statistics Canada figures show that 25 per cent of the people employed in the Churchill riding are directly employed in the primary industries, with almost every other job in the riding indirectly related to those industries.
April 2, 1987

Farmers in the Carrot River Valley, forestry workers in The Pas, miners in Flin Flon, Snow Lake, Thompson, Lynn Lake and Leaf Rapids, CN railway workers, all are dependent upon export markets.
Manitoba is an exporter of hydro-electric power, so hydro workers at Gillam and construction workers at the Limestone Power Project are dependent upon export markets for their livelihood.
With so many people in the Churchill riding dependent upon export markets, and particularly U.S. markets, I am surprised that the Member for Churchill is not supportive of our trade talks with the U.S.
Free trade will be good for the residents of Churchill riding, as it will be for all Canadians. The Member for Churchill should stand up for his constituents, instead of blindly following his anti-American socialist Leader, the Member for Oshawa (Mr. Broadbent).

maintopic: STATISTICAL BREAKDOWN OF CHILDREN REQUIRING DAY CARE
STATISTICAL BREAKDOWN OF CHILDREN REQUIRING DAY CARE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise to speak to the day care crisis in Canada, a crisis of which we have all been made very much aware during the past few days, and a crisis defined as being the need for 1.9 million day care spaces for Canadian children.
When day care advocates refer to the 2.1 million children in Canada who require day care spaces, their figures include all children under 12, where both parents work full or part-time, or where one spouse attends school for more than 20 hours per week.
Of the 2.1 million children referred to by the Opposition, I have discovered that over 1 million-actually, 1.1 million, to be precise-are children of school age.
While most of my colleagues in the House would agree that "latch key" children require some assistance, surely it is misleading to assume that all of these children are suffering from a day care crisis.

subtopic: REJECTION OF ATTEMPT TO REINSTATE DEATH PENALTY IN BRITAIN
REJECTION OF ATTEMPT TO REINSTATE DEATH PENALTY IN BRITAIN
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, yesterday the Mother of Parliaments showed us the way. The British House of Commons voted by a margin of 112 to defeat a proposed amendment to restore the death penalty for certain acts of murder in Britain.
Why is this important to Canada? It is important because the public mood in Canada is similar to that of Britain where about 70 per cent favour the death penalty. Our role is not to ignore public opinion but to make dispassionate decisions on public policy based on all the facts.
Why has Britain rejected the death penalty? British Members of Parliament said no to capital punishment because they know it is not a deterrent to murder. British MPs said no because they know innocent people have been executed. British MPs said no because they know that juries often fail to convict murderers if the accused is to be executed. British MPs said no because they know that many terrorists crave martyrdom. I suspect that British MPs said no because they know that it is wrong for the state, for the Government, to execute a human being.

April 2, 1987

speakeroldname: Mr. Lawrence I. O'Neil (Cape Breton Highlands-Canso):
subtopic: CANADA-NOVA SCOTIA LIVESTOCK FEED DEVELOPMENT PROGRAM
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, a joint Canada-Nova Scotia Livestock Feed Development Agreement was signed at the federal-provincial agriculture Ministers' meeting in Ottawa on Monday.
Nova Scotia's livestock industry has been highly dependent on outside sources of feed grains and protein crops. Because of rising transportation costs, this dependence has been seriously threatening the competitive position of livestock producers.
The Nova Scotia agreement includes programs geared specifically to the province's need to attain a high level of livestock feed self-sufficiency by the year 2000. The agreement will help ensure that livestock producers who grow their own feed, or feed producers who sell feed, can do so with the lowest possible cost of production.
In Nova Scotia's case, $11.25 million in funding will be made available. The federal Government will provide 80 per cent of this amount and the province the remaining 20 per cent.
This agreement proves that subsidies can be replaced by sensible programs which will achieve self-sufficiency. I congratulate the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Wise) for responding to the needs of Nova Scotia farmers and the requests of the Nova Scotia caucus.

The House resumed consideration of Bill C-22, an Act to amend the Patent Act and to provide for certain matters in relation thereto, as reported (with amendments) from a legislative committee, and Motions No. 3 (Mr. Dingwall), No. 4 (Mr. Orlikow) and Nos. 5, 11, 13 and 15 (Mr. Dingwall, p. 4820).

Madam Speaker, I am pleased to have the opportunity to speak on this second grouping of motions, and particularly on the motion put forward by my colleague, the Hon. Member for Winnipeg North (Mr. Orlikow).
Contrary to the information that was purported to be found in a sponsored poll, I do not think the majority of Canadians support this legislation at all, and the more they find out about it the less they are going to support it.
The fact is that up until 1969, when changes were made to the Patent Act that allowed for the production of generic drugs, Canada and Canadians were paying the second highest
April 2, 1987

prices in the industrialized world for prescription drugs. As a result of the changes that allowed for the production of generic drugs in Canada, Canadians are now paying the second lowest prices in the industrialized world for prescription drugs.The change in the price that is being paid for drugs, Madam Speaker, is directly attributable to the change in legislation which allowed for the production of generic drugs, and we do not want to see that forward move turned backwards. The Government apparently does.
The Government apparently has concerns, has priorities, other than the health of Canadians. The importance of prescription drugs to the millions of Canadians who depend upon them in helping them to deal with one health problem or another cannot be underestimated, and the costs of such drugs is of major concern to Canadians. Also, it is of major concern to provincial health care programs and provincial pharmacare programs. It is estimated that without generic drugs the costs of provincial pharmacare programs would increase by at least 20 per cent.
In Bill C-22 we are faced with legislation that is going to change that very positive provision that allowed for the production of generic drugs. This legislation would turn the clock backwards. Canadian people have to ask themselves why it is that the Government is doing this. It seems that it is some kind of fancy foreplay to the consummation of the free trade talks. It is in line with the elimination of FIRA; it is in line with the Government buckling under to the Americans on any number of issues.
The fact is, there has been a great deal of pressure from the American pharmaceutical industry and from the American Government to have the Canadian Government bring in these changes. That pressure was first applied to the Liberal Government. Some members of that Government were prepared to go along with it; others decided that they would try to stall it, and to that end they introduced the Eastman Commission. When the Eastman commission reported in June of 1985, it made significant recommendations, recommendations that I think completely cut the ground from under those who would turn the clock and make it more difficult to introduce generic drugs.
On the one hand, the Government is facing pressure from the American Government and the pharmaceutical companies to turn the clock back; on the other hand, the members of the New Democratic Party, along with Canadians from one coast to the other, have been rallying around this issue trying to emphasize the need to maintain the provisions of the Patent Act that allow for the production of generic drugs.
I have received countless letters in my office. Other members of the New Democratic Party caucus have received a number of letters, and I know that members of the other Parties have as well, including a great many Members on the government side. Why they are not acting on the basis of those letters, I do not know.
Patent Act
We have also had many petitions tabled in this regard. Some of the Progressive Conservative Members have been a little bit skittish about the tabling of some of these petitions, because they indicate very clearly that there is a very great concern about the way in which these very positive provisions in respect of the production of generic drugs are being negated by Bill C-22.
We are concerned, Madam Speaker, with Motion No. 4, among others, which would limit the exclusivity of patent protection of newly introduced drugs to four years. This four-year provision is a bit of a compromise. It is what was recommended by the Eastman Commission report. It is a much better provision than the provision in the legislation, which allows for 10 years.
The Eastman Commission points out the importance of some period of exclusivity. I should like to read a short passage from the Eastman report;
The pricing behaviour of firms introducing new drugs in the Canadian market and abroad is typically to set high prices initially when the novelty and uniqueness of the drug is greatest so as to maximize its profitability. As competition develops from imitative drugs either with patents of their own or as generics in Canada, prices tend to decline and so increase the benefit of the new drug to consumers and taxpayers.
An assurance of monopoly in the market at the most profitable early period after the introduction of a new drug ensures a satisfactory return and therefore constitutes an inducement to introduce the drug in Canada.
The Eastman report recognizes that there should be some period of protection for a new drug. It continues:
The question is to decide on the appropriate length of a period of exclusivity during which the innovating firm can charge prices well above the cost of materials and manufacturing to create a gross profit that covers all other costs including the high initial promotion costs.
The question is, what is the optimum period for monopoly protection? The Eastman Commission dealt with that wherein the report indicated:
The Commission was told at the Hearings by representatives of Merck Frosst that many drugs achieved large sales in the first year following their introduction and that drugs that took longest to establish themselves required from three to four years after which the growth in their sales slowed. This view is consistent with other information. The four-year of exclusivity that the Commission believes should be given new drugs reflects these estimates.
In other words, this four-year exclusivity period reflected in Motion No. 4 has not been pulled out of a hat. It was based upon the testimony of a pharmaceutical drug company before the Eastman Commission which indicated that the longest time it took for a drug to establish itself was some four years. It gives adequate protection for new drugs coming on the market.
We recognize that that is important. There should be adequate protection, but we do not think that there should be the kind of protection which allows drug companies to continue making profits after profits to the detriment of Canadians who must purchase the drugs.
In Bill C-22 the Government wants to give a period of 10 years of exclusivity for the manufacturers of drugs. Over a period of 10 years the makers of brand name drugs will then

The American Association of Retired Persons was invited by members of my Party to appear before the legislative committee on Bill C-22. The Conservatives refused to allow the association to appear because they did not want to hear testimony from Americans about the way in which the system in the United States works to the detriment of average Americans who must purchase drugs.
I see that my time is up. I simply urge government Members to consider the implications of what they are trying to do by granting a 10-year period of exclusivity. It will mean that drug prices will remain high. They should look at the recommendations of the Eastman Commission which suggested a four-year period, based upon some solid reasons. They should listen to the voices of their constituents who urge them not to take this action which will result in higher drug prices for them and for their fellow Canadians. I urge government Members to pay attention to these issues.

Madam Speaker, I welcome this opportunity to speak to Bill C-22 and to defend the amendments proposed by the Liberal Party. I am referring to Motions numbered 3, 4, 5, 11, 13 and 15. In these motions we talked about the period of exclusivity. The Bill is proposing a 10 year exclusivity period, and as all members know perfectly well, we in the Liberal Party are proposing four years, as recommended by the Eastman report. As for the date of proclamation, the House will recall that in 1986, the Government was unable to follow through on its Bill. However, in the Bill tabled on November 6, the proclamation date remained unchanged, which means that the legislation is retroactive, which is totally unacceptable. It means that the legislation is retroactive to June 1986.
And finally, regarding the motion on the priority status for process and product patents, we are proposing this amendment because it will have a very definite impact on development in the technology sector.
I would like to start by discussing the period of exclusivity. As I said earlier, the Eastman report recommended a period of exclusivity of four years. The reason was simple. According to the Commission of Inquiry, it was necessary to encourage pharmaceutical companies to do research. The Commission was well aware of the pattern followed by pharmaceutical companies: as soon as they enjoy too much protection, they tend to waste the funds this protection affords them. This argument is part of the Eastman report and Hon. Members will find it on page 338.
Indeed, Madam Speaker, there is a description of the consequences of too little and too much protection. I quote from page 338:
Another consequence of excessive patent protection and of the profits to which
it potentially gives rise is to induce patent holders-
-the multinationals in this case-
-to incur excessive costs of promotion through marketing and selling
expenditures designed to stimulate demand and maintain their competitive
position in the market.
Madam Speaker, it seems to me the Minister completely forgot this fact when he decided to give 10 years of exclusivity. This is a striking example of a recommendation which was totally ignored, and it flies in the face of a serious study which cost Canadians a pretty penny.
When he refused to answer our questions in the House the Minister promised he would give the committee all data on which he had based his decision. We soon realized he had no intention of doing that. The Minister simply told the committee that fours years of exclusivity was too short, and that was that. Where did he get this information? We did not find out in committee. I am sure that not one Conservative Member can tell me either, and that none of the departmental officials can give me a rational explanation. Why 10 instead of four years? Why not follow the Eastman recommendation? The only ones in a position to give us the answer are the multinationals because this decision gives them the upper hand.
A 10 year exclusivity period will have an impact on the profits of those companies. In fact, in his report Mr. Eastman provided a documented and wide-ranging explanation of the phenomenon associated with the protection a patent may afford. According to him, new drugs are always priced high to recoup development costs.
The shorter the exclusivity period, the higher the introductory price. When the exclusivity period is longer, the introductory price is lower, but it takes much longer to decrease.
My question is as follows: Is there anyone in the House who has made an assessment of the impact the Conservative Government's policy will have? How do we know which option will cost more? A short or a long period of exclusivity? No assessment has been made. Government Members may argue that the Opposition is wrong to say it will be expensive and that prices will go up, but what contribution has the Government made to this debate? Not a single Conservative has had the guts to rise in the House to speak to this Bill.
And furthermore, we have no indication of the impact the measures proposed by the Government will have aside from a partisan study by the Department.
Madam Speaker, Mr. Bill Haddad, a representative of the U.S. generic drugs industry who was refused permission to appear before the Committee, nevertheless came to Canada to describe to us the situation in the United States. He pointed out that research and development for most of the drugs originating in the United States had already been paid for by U.S. citizens. In fact, the multinationals were making so much
April 2, 1987

money they were researching the best ways to invest their excess profits. Considering all these factors, we can hardly accept a period of exclusivity for the duration proposed in the Bill.
As we all know, the Bill does not take into consideration the consumers of pharmaceutical products, and even worse, it fails to consider the needs of the biotechnological industry in Canada. I find it very difficult to accept the Government's defence of the need to adopt legislation that is similar to legislation in effect in the international community. The Government could have accepted, and it can still do so, the Liberal Party's amendment by which not only product but also process patents would be allowed as far as the biotechnological industry is concerned. This is a complex part of our amendments, but I wanted to have them included in the proceedings of the House because I think they are important. If the Government does not accept these amendments, it will be showing itself to be insensitive in the extreme and lacking in any understanding for the needs and the nature of the biotechnological industry in Canada.
Finally, I would like to talk about the drugs which, at the time the Government announced its intention to amend the Act last June, were still in the "pipeline". There were a number of specific provisions for the so-called pipeline drugs. In the new version of this Bill, the Bill that was tabled in the House several months ago in June, there have been no changes. An attempt was made to table the Bill in June and it was finally tabled in November, but nothing was changed which means that the Bill will be retroactive to June 27, 1986. That we cannot accpet. They could at least have changed this date for the date on which the present Bill was tabled, or as we state in our amendment, substitute the date of the royal proclamation. Once again, the Government has caved in to pressure from the multinationals.
This Bill does nothing at all for the whole sector of the generic and biotechnological industries, quite the contrary. This is why we are proposing an amendment to that effect. I want this to be very clear.
The 10 year exclusivity period is unacceptable, we believe that the four-year period recommended by the Eastman Commission is reasonable. Several interest groups share this view and gave us their support in the parliamentary committee. It is interesting to note that most interest groups are aware that it is necessary to provide better intellectual protection for patents, and this explains why they are prepared to accept changes to the legislation which dates back to 1969. Of course, they too realize the need for better protection, but they all agree that a 10 year period is too long and unwarranted. However a number of them would endorse the four-year period advocated by the Eastman Commission simply because most interest groups are reasonable and realistic.
The generic sector of the pharmaceutical industry told us it could quite probably have lived with a four-year exclusivity period for patent holders. We must bear in mind that the generic industry is the industry which copies.

My time has expired, Madam Speaker. Very well, I must accept your decision. I will be back for the next amendment. Thank you, Madam Speaker.

Madam Speaker, I am pleased to have an opportunity to speak to this particular motion. It refers to the problem about which many Canadians have registered concern time and time again through petitions, namely, that this Bill will give exclusive rights, I like to call it monopoly rights, to drug companies, largely foreign multinational drug companies, over a particular drug, which will result in higher costs than they would be under a competitive system. It does not take any imagination to recognize that if you have exclusive rights, monopoly control, you will not take advantage of that monopoly if you are in the business to make profits, to distribute to your shareholders. That situation, however, will occur in Canada in the future. I think back to the beginnings of the Canadian economy when the Hudson's Bay Company of Canada was given sole monopoly over the fur trading areas of all the lands drained by rivers going into Hudson's Bay. You could not compete with the Hudson's Bay in that area.
I find it surprising that the Minister with whom we are dealing in this matter is the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs (Mr. Andre). Presumably the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs is interested in competition in the market-place to keep the prices of prescription drugs as low as possible. One of the very tenets on which the Progressive Conservative Party exists is a commitment, belief and value of competition in the market-place. I have heard hundreds of speeches in this House that try to remind us all that competition of almost any kind is good. Yet this Bill is totally contrary to that because it excludes competition for 10 years. You would be aware, Madam Speaker, that it was Dr. Eastman himself, the author of the original study conducted by the then Minister of Consumer and Corporation Affairs in the Liberal Government, who suggested that it would be fair for a drug company, having discovered a new drug, to have a monopoly for four years in order to benefit from the research money invested. All right, one could perhaps make that case, but this Bill extends the monopoly not for four years but for 10 years. That perplexes many of us, and that is why we oppose this aspect of the Bill.
Time and time again during this debate Members on the government side have referred to a recent poll. It indicates, as it is alleged, that eight in 10 Canadians are in favour of the Government passing Bill C-22. This is a very serious problem as I see it. The poll released was commissioned by the Pharmaceutical Manufacturers Association and done through Decima Research. If you look at the poll itself, it is printed on the letterhead of the Pharmaceutical Manufacturers Association of Canada. All of the people one is asked to contact for further information are people with the association or the PR

April 2, 1987
Patent Act
people for the association. This poll done by Decima was not an objective poll. The poll differs from any other that I have ever seen. I really wonder about Decima because it often prides itself on being on objective polling agency. We know it does a lot of work for the Conservative Party and we know that the Conservative Party is interested in getting this Bill through as rapidly as possible.
Consider the bias, Madam Speaker, which surprises me. Social scientists who conduct these polls pride themselves on devising questions that are as value-free and as bias-free as possible. We know that it is probably impossible to be free of bias, but there are degrees of bias that could be tolerated. In the Decima poll, Canadians were asked to respond to this statement: "If brand name companies double research efforts in Canada, health care and quality of life will improve because of early access to new, high quality cures". Of course an average Canadian would support such a statement. However, I would like to know if this statement is even correct. It is loaded with unproven statements and real bias.
There is nothing in the Bill compelling companies to double research efforts. The companies simply say that they will increase research and development efforts by 10 per cent of sales by 1995. We know better than to suggest that companies like these could be taken at their word. If this is serious and the companies mean what they say, why not put in the legislation that this is a commitment to research and development in Canada that the pharmaceutical industry is prepared to make? The legislation is mute in this respect.
There is no guarantee that this research will be basic scientific research. We have heard that much of the research that will be taking place in Canada will be market and clinical research, with basic research being only about 10 per cent of all research. We will see research into how best to market pills, how to get more mileage out of a certain coloured pill. That is not the kind of scientific research we want to have take place in Canada as a result of the monopoly control that these companies will have.
The primary objective of pharmaceutical research is to produce drugs that are big sellers. Let us not kid ourselves by believing that this is not so. The best way to produce these drugs is by imitating best-selling drugs using a slightly different chemical structure for what is known as a minor therapeutic gain. There is nothing in the legislation that will guarantee research. As a matter of fact, as we know from previous debate in the House, there is not even a definition of research in the Bill.
For this poll to suggest that research will take place once this Bill is passed is highly questionable. Quite frankly, I do not think it does the credibility of the Decima polling organization any good at all. In fact, an allegation of asking highly biased questions is very, very serious.
I would like to refer to what I believe is a much more appropriate poll taken by Reid. Some weeks ago, this organization asked Canadians to respond to this statement:
As you may know, the Government recently presented legislation which will give drug companies exclusive patent rights to manufacture and sell the drugs they invented for a longer period of time than they have now. Other companies will not be allowed to produce or sell less expensive copies of most drugs for 10 years. Do you yourself support or oppose this proposed legislation?
The results were interesting. In Canada as a whole, 58 per cent were opposed and 30 per cent supported it. In British Columbia, 66 per cent were opposed to it, in Alberta, 62 per cent were opposed to it, and in Manitoba and Saskatchewan, 69 per cent were opposed to it. In Ontario and Quebec, 54 per cent were opposed to it and in Atlantic Canada, 56 per cent were opposed to it. When Canadians were asked if they believe that multinational drug companies operating in Canada ought to have exclusive rights and monopoly control to sell their new products for 10 years, eliminating any competition in the drug market-place, thank goodness an overwhelming number of Canadians said no.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Liberal Party
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I welcome this opportunity to take part at this stage in the debate on Bill C-22. Perhaps I should remind the House that we are now on the amendments that were regrouped by the Chair and which deal with-amendments Nos. 3 . . . I'm trying to find the page, I won't be long. Meanwhile, Madam Speaker, I would like to say it is always easy to use the polls to support a point one wants to make, and in fact I too was surprised that the Government would use a poll ordered by the multinationals to justify Bill C-22, especially since we all know that in January and last year, a poll by the Reid Report and another by Gallup clearly indicated that Canadians were very much opposed to this Bill. According to the Reid Report, 58 per cent of Canadians were opposed to this legislation. The question that was put to Canadians was quite clear: Do you support this Bill? In the Decima poll referred to by the previous speaker, the question put by the company conducting the poll was somewhat different. The question was:

"After hearing all the various arguments in favour and against the proposed Bill," even though we are not finished arguing the Bill, "is it your impression that the Bill is a very good thing, a good thing, a bad thing or a very bad thing?"

Madam Speaker, obviously, Canadians were going to say what they thought and do so freely, but it is not very convincing when we know there were two polls, one by Gallup and the other by Reid, that produced the opposite results, while today we have a poll that says that perhaps Canadians think it might not be such a bad idea to review the provisions for protecting pharmaceutical companies and allow them to retain patent rights on certain drugs.
April 2, 1987

In any case, Madam Speaker, we object because we believe-and we have always supported the Eastman report that was ordered by the previous Government and which recommends a period of four years. We think that is satisfactory and sufficient, and we believe, polls or no polls, that people should listen to the points we have to make before jumping to conclusions.

The ruling having been made, we are discussing Motions Nos. 3, 4, 5, 11, 13 and 15. These motions deal with a radical, retrograde proposal of product rather than process patents for pharmaceutical products. In the past, process patents have allowed generic companies which produce low cost copies of medications to improve upon methods of creating drugs for their own ease in producing the drugs and for gaining an advantage over competitors by producing the drugs in question at lower costs. The innovation process was endless and enormously beneficial to Canada.
We in Canada are very proud of having one of the best health care systems in the world. It is highly recognized for its quality, its universality and its transferability from province to province. It is accessible to all Canadians and, of course, it is non-profit, something of which we are very proud. We cannot say that that is the reality in the United States. We know that in the United States, there is no national health care program accessible to all Americans in a universal fashion. It is not transferable and it is therefore very difficult sometimes to be faced with sickness and disease. In Canada we feel very comfortable with the very sound system of health care we have developed over the years. That system is based not only on the services rendered by health practitioners, but also on access to a solid range of pharmaceuticals.
The myth that if we pass this Bill there will be $1.4 billion of research and development in pharmaceutical products sounds good. It looks fine on paper. However, we have never seen any commitment from the industry and we have yet to hear from the Minister how he will hold them to that commitment if it does exist. We are a small but proud country. We are not a large market, but we are a stable and very good market. As far as we in the Liberal Party are concerned, we have been very well served over the years by both the generic and the multinational drug companies which operate within our borders. The Eastman report was needed and the recommendations in it should be followed.
To get back to the amendments and what I call the radical retrograde step of proposing product rather than process patents for pharmaceutical products, what we are trying to do is to delete product patents from the legislation. As the law now stands, only process patents can be granted. Bill C-22 would allow product patents to be granted as well. Canadian biotechnology firms say that this change will effectively put them out of business. I want to refer to the transcript of the committee hearing of January 29, 1987, where a company
Patent Act
called Cangene appeared. That company developed a drug, Interleuken 2. For those who are interested, when mixed with a prostaglandin inhibitor it looks as though it will be a real cancer cure. It reverses in-place, solid tumours. This is what the company said:
Cangene is one of the few companies in the world that can do this, and we are ready to move to scale-up to clinical trials, and to manufacture. We have succeeded in this one instance, and there may be more, using Canadian ingenuity and Canadian money, operating under Canadian law.
It goes on and, referring to the Government, says:
On the verge of our success, you propose to change the rules. Under the new rules, the Cangene process, already successful with one and perhaps successful with others yet to be tried, will be useless.
It will be useless, because you, in the amendments, will allow product patents. The natural health-giving proteins will become the private property of a single company. The process used to make that protein, the Cangene process, will be immaterial.
Under your new rules or the rules proposed in the amendments, the battle for the market-place will move into the courtroom, as it has in the United States. That will doom Cangene and Canada forever-from establishing a Canadian niche in the protein-based pharmaceutical manufacturing industry. Surely together we can write legislation which will not throw out the baby, Cangene, with the bath water.
My time has expired, Madam Speaker. I would like to continue on the next amendment.

Madam Speaker, the issue addressed in the amendments presently under discussion is that of intellectual property. Before examining the contrast between the Eastman report's recommendations and the Government's proposals in Bill C-22, let us once more remind ourselves of the impetus behind this legislation resulting from pressure exerted from south of our border.
Both you and Canadians generally know the history of the cosy get-together between the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) and the President a couple of years ago which set this legislation in train. You will know of the frequent interventions of Mr. Yeutter to encourage Canada to recognize something called intellectual property. It was argued that Canadians offend against that property right held by Americans by virtue of our present patent legislation. You will know, too, that the U.S. Vice-President is a former member of the board of directors of one of the largest drug manufacturing companies in the U.S., to wit, Eli Lilly. You will also know that the Chairman of the President's Advisory Committee on Trade, E. J. Pratt, was president of another large U.S. multinational with interests in Canada. You will know that the legislation before us then represents an effort on the part of the Government to meet the demands imposed upon it by the Americans as a condition to the free trade negotiations in which the Government is presently engaged. You will know that in every respect the Government has, with great urgency, attempted to fulfil every demand placed upon it by the Americans.
It is interesting to note that the present legislation, which does so much offence to our system of public health, is not enough. You are as familiar as every other Member of Parliament with the list of demands the Americans have been mandated to make at these negotiations. Still appearing among those demands, irrespective of the existence of Bill C-22, is increased protection for American intellectual property. That includes their opinion that the legislation we are discussing today is not enough. Therefore, if Canadians are watching this debate with the assumption that Bill C-22 is all the harm that the Government will perpetrate upon them, then I am saying, and they ought to know, that there may yet be more of an attack on the system of drug availability which heretofore has been so consistent with the Canadian assumption that health services ought to be available to all irrespective of cost. I am sure you recognize that that is not an imperative in the American system.
It has been alleged by members on the other side, including the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs (Mr. Andre) that in opposing this legislation New Democrats are somehow opposed to the concept of intellectual property. This is, of
course, unmitigated nonsense. Intellectual property is not something which can always be bought and sold. We are talking about intellectual property which leads to some kind of product, some sort of good which reflects the productivity of creativity.
You and I know, Madam Speaker, that if one examines the history of intellectual artistic endeavour one will see that the most fundamental contributions have not led to patents or to a penny. Surely everyone in the House recognizes that when Newton conceived of a way in which to express the relationship between material bodies his notion about gravity did not lead to any patent. To be even more relevant to the present discussion, let us reflect upon the discovery by Fleming of penicillin. The discovery of penicillin did not lead to a significant penny for Mr. Fleming. When Selman Waksman discovered streptomycin there was a patent and royalties were paid for it, but they did not go exclusively into the pockets of the corporation. They went to the universities and led to more discoveries in the area of antibiotics. Selman Waksman gained only a modest living therefrom.
The concept of patents is, of course, to provide some stimulus for making available to the general population products of intellectual effort and to provide a stimulus for making those products available in the market-place. It is for the convenience of the population at large and for the stimulation of those who, by virtue of their intellectual endeavours, create something which might benefit the population, to encourage that kind of creativity, but it is not absolute. It has never been conceived of as absolute. If it were absolute, patents would exist in perpetuity as would exclusivity, and they do not.
The reality is that when exclusivity existed for 14 years prior to 1969, the drug companies used this protection literally to steal money out of the pockets of the poor. Their profits were unquestionably excessive. The robbery imposed upon those who needed medicine was vicious. A situation was created in which it was clear to everyone that something had to be done to change the situation. As a result, in 1969 the present legislation was adopted by the Parliament and the Government of the time. There followed a period during which Canada became the heir of the best arrangement in the world for making drugs available to those who needed them. You will, of course, recognize that the mechanism was the compulsory licensing of generic drugs.
According to the arguments presented by the Government one might have thought that the multinationals must have virtually gone into bankruptcy, that they were looking at poverty as a result of the legislation. The fact is that their profits changed not a whit. In 1985, they averaged 22 per cent, and one of them had profits over sales of 51 per cent. Therefore, they are profitable. In fact, this sector is more profitable than any other manufacturing sector.
One must ask why the Government would suggest 10 years of exclusivity. Why were the recommendations of Eastman ignored? Why would a Government respond not to the needs
April 2, 1987

of the people, not to the recommendations of a well and carefully prepared report, but to the demands of an American Government? It is sinful that a Government would behave in such a way. One must remember that this is a Government which 78 per cent of the population regards as an appropriate Party for the Opposition. I, too, share with the Canadian people their hope that some day the Party which is in government now will be as effective in opposition when we are in government as this Party is today.

Madam Speaker, I rise to speak on Motions Nos. 3, 4, 5, 11, 13 and 15. These motions fall into two general areas. Motions Nos. 3, 13 and 15 profoundly affect the Canadian biotechnological firms which see this legislation as a grave threat to their survival. Motions Nos. 4, 5, and 11 fall into another grouping. Motion No. 3 deals with a subsection which reads:
(b) where the invention is other than a process, to make or use the invention
for medicine or for the preparation or production of medicine-
These motions are asking for the removal of these sections. I wish the Government would appreciate what the impact upon the biotechnological industry in Canada will be if these sections are not removed.
These motions are moved by the Member for Cape Breton- East Richmond (Mr. Dingwall) who has been spending a great deal of time listening to and studying the representations made by Canadian and multinational drug producers as well as all the organizations and people who will be adversely affected by the general trend and development of the Bill itself. The Bill is a threat, not only to companies operating in Canada and the pharmaceutical business, but also to the taxpayer, the provinces, and their budgets.
It is a particular threat to those in weaker positions, the elderly, those more prone to the need for drugs, those who are handicapped and disabled, and to poorer people of our population. It is certainly a threat to the disadvantaged groups which often turn out to be various people of certain races in areas of our country which are economically deprived. I am thinking, of course, at this moment of our native Canadians whom we have already so badly disappointed. There is already a crushing burden in so many ways upon those who are weak and poor in our society and the regions of our country which are not benefiting from the present increase in employment. The benefits being enjoyed in the Golden Elorseshoe are not being enjoyed in areas like Newfoundland and British Columbia. It is for these disadvantaged that we speak because any increase in the cost of drugs ultimately, whether in the short run or the long run, will be a source of suffering for them.
We can talk about providing, perhaps, more research, and that case has not, to my mind, been proven. But even if there were more research in Canada, that does not solve the problem of the suffering that higher drug prices will mean to those who are poorer and less advantaged. It is for them that the Bill,
Patent Act
which allowed Canadian companies to enter into the generic drug field after a reasonable period of time, was originally passed, so there would then be that kind of fair competition which would allow people in Canada to buy drugs at a reasonable price.
Members of our Party certainly are not opposed, in fact, welcome the idea that there be some decent profit for those companies which have had the courage to go into private enterprise and do the research for drugs and bring them on the market. Obviously, if we did not give some kind of rewards to such companies there would be no reason for them to do the research they do. At the same time, it seems to us Draconian to think we are going to give such complete protection to multinational foreign companies to continue almost endlessly, at least for the living life of the drug itself, to charge the kinds of prices they wish to charge.
I know the Government will say there are some forms of protection so that drug prices will not be unreasonable. Even those who are involved confess that it will be quite some time before the hearings are completed, before the value of the drug is really assessed, and we are not at all persuaded that through such a long process the interests of the public will be served, especially those who are less well off financially.
It seems like a tragic form of inverted logic, or a form of hoodwinking, when Members of the Government try to persuade the Canadian people that a 10 year protection is something that is required in order to provide worth-while research in this field. We know that multinational companies have been profiting rather well. We know they are still selling their products in this country. We certainly feel there is a need for some kind of fair competition.
We have been trying as a Party to follow the recommendations of the Eastman Commission which studied this matter. It suggests that there be a moderate approach to this whole question. On the one hand there would be respect for the need for research and adequate encouragement and, on the other hand, generic drugs would be provided to the Canadian public in a reasonable time period. Because of policies we have followed up to this time, Canadians have profited by lower drug costs. We have one of the best pricing systems in the world. Yet, the research which has been done has not been any less. In fact, I think we can, if we wish, provide incentives to Canadian companies to carry on research here. There would be plenty of opportunity to do so.
What will happen if this Government's Bill is passed, ultimately, is that multinational corporations will make a large profit, and the Canadian public will not be protected by the possibility of lower generic drugs being brought on the market, which means they will pay higher prices than they otherwise would. All of the abracadabra of the Minister who tries to play around with these words about what is more or less, will not fool the Canadian public one bit. If there is no competition through generic drugs we know that drugs will cost more than they otherwise would if there were generic drugs available. It is that simple and logical. Therefore, when we say that the cost

April 2, 1987
Patent Act
of drugs will be higher, that is what they will be, higher than if the Government did not pass this Bill. If this Bill is not passed, the cost of drugs will not go up, and they will cost more if this Government's Bills are passed in future years.
The cost of health care is going to increase over the years as we have a larger and larger aging population. We still have not come under this Government's great era of supposed economic improvement. The same number of people are at the poverty line. As the provinces try to pay the cost of drugs to take care of those who, in larger numbers, are going to need those drugs, obviously the taxpayers are going to have to pay more money. Canadians will have to pay more money at the pharmacy. I do not think the pharmaceutical industry enjoys one bit having to charge more. I am sure it has appreciated the pleasure of seeing the availability of drugs to the senior citizens and poorer people.
I would suggest that the Government should go back to the drawing board and at least consider these amendments which are before it for consideration. I hope these amendments will be allowed to pass.

Madam Speaker, I am very glad to have a chance to speak on this group of amendments. The amendment I am promoting, of course, is Motion No. 4. This clause of the Bill would give a monopoly of up to 10 years, depending on circumstances, to the producer or manufacturer of a new drug. Our amendment would reduce that monopoly to four years. This is based on the study by Professor Eastman which received a very wide consensus in the country. He argued there should be some time protection for the patent, but not as much as 10 years. He recommended four years on the basis of intensive study. Why? He said that at the end of four years it was appropriate to let competition from the generic drug industry, which by now is well established in Canada and employs many people, lower or at least prevent a rise in price. His study estimates that in 1983 alone the present legislation saved people $211 million. This means senior citizens, young people, and persons who are mainly dependent on these drugs, would have paid $211 million more in total had the present generic drug legislation not been in place. That is the kind of benefit that will be considerably lost if this new legislation goes through without our amendment which would restore some protection to the consumers.
The point of view of the Government of Canada, the Government of the United States and the multinational profit drug industry, is that not only will they lose money-which they do not emphasize very much-but they will not create so many jobs in Canada, they will not produce new drugs in Canada and there will be higher prices than otherwise for any new drugs which are produced in Canada or elsewhere. We cannot take those arguments seriously. The fact is that the drug industry, which promised 3,000 new professional class jobs, turned out to be flim-flamming the public through the Minister. Only 1,148 professional jobs will be created. The large majority of the 3,000 jobs would be lower clerical and manual jobs. Of course, the industry does not mention that by
doing this the pharmaceutical multinationals would destroy or cut back the generic drug industry in Canada. This means that many jobs could be lost if the Bill passes without the adoption of the amendments we have proposed.
According to a study by the Consumers' Association of Canada the multinationals are doing very well at the present time in Canada in terms of their prices and their profits. If they wanted to establish research in Canada they have the profits with which to do it. When they say that to continue with the 1969 legislation would cost us these new jobs, they ignore the fact that before the 1969 legislation was enacted there were 12,645 jobs in the drug industry, almost none of them in the generic firms. However, in 1982, after the legislation had been in force for 13 years, there were 15,707 jobs, about 1,300 of them in generic firms. Thus if the 1969 legislation had any effect on employment, it was to encourage an increase of about 25 per cent or 3,000 new jobs.
With respect to whether research and development has slowed, the fact is that very little research was being done before 1969. There is little reason to suppose that the multinationals will change their habits. They now have highly centralized world-wide production with high technology and low labour components. It is not likely that out of friendship they will establish many operations in Canada that will produce jobs, especially good jobs. By the same token, it is not likely that they will develop any new drugs in Canada. They were not doing that before. With respect to new drug prices being lower if they are granted a 10-year monopoly, that has absolutely no basis in terms of the experience before 1969. So there is no reason to think that if we give the multinational drug companies a 10-year monopoly there will be any benefit to Canadians in terms of drug prices or in terms of new drugs.
With respect to the benefit in terms of jobs, there could very well be more jobs lost than gained. If they do put in place 3,000 new jobs, that would only balance the 3,000 jobs that were created as a result of the 1969 legislation. Such a move would simply replace those 3,000 jobs. So there would be no net gain in terms of jobs.
The best arrangement would be to keep the old Bill in place, or to make more cautious changes to it. If the new Bill is introduced, we will need the amendment which we are now discussing, which would cut the monopoly from 10 years to four years. Monopolies are a fact of life. Bell Canada is a monopoly. We all know the difficulty consumers have in terms of getting a fair shake for a fair price out of Bell. The gas companies are near monopolies. We all know the difficulties we have in seeing any real competition which would lower the price of gas. It will be the same among these multinational drug companies. They now bring in a profit of between 22 per cent and 59 per cent per year. They do not really need to take any more money from the senior citizens and the children of Canada who are the main beneficiaries of prescription drugs.

We have a good health system in Canada as compared to the United States, which is the home of the majority of the multinationals which deal in Canada. The health system costs less per person in Canada than it does in the United States. In fact, it produces a higher level of health for the people of Canada than the American system produces for its people. We are getting far more for our money in terms of health care than the people of the United States are getting for theirs. Part of the system that has produced this benefit for the people of Canada has been a result of the generic drug legislation which was passed in 1969 which kept a reasonable ceiling on the price of prescription drugs. Therefore, this amendment is to the benefit of millions of ordinary Canadians. It far outweighs any doubtful claim that the Government or the multinationals can make, or that President Reagan can make when he leans on our Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney), that giving still more money to the monopolies will create extra jobs and new drugs and would, by some magic that the monopolies have never demonstrated, bring drug prices down.
I urge the House to adopt Motion No. 4 and the other amendments which are in the same spirit which would prevent the destruction, the erosion of the present generic drug legislation which has been of such benefit to Canadians during the last 18 years and which is basically very much needed by all Canadians, but in particular those most at risk, that is, senior citizens and children.
