speechtext:
Madam Speaker, in speaking to this motion, I would like first to congratulate the Hon. Member for Grey-Simcoe (Mr. Mitges) for his continuous and courageous defence of the rights of the unborn child. I would also like to congratulate those who have spoken before me in favour of this motion. They have dealt with it in an eloquent and convincing manner on behalf of the unborn child. In particular, I would like to congratulate the seat-mate I first had when I came to the House, the Hon. Member for Willowdale (Mr. Oostrom), who on several occasions has spoken in support of the rights of the unborn child. I would also like to congratulate my present seat-mate, the Hon. Member for Niagara Falls (Mr. Nicholson).
During my election campaign, a pro-life debate was held and candidates were asked to put forward their positions on the important question of the rights of unborn children. In that debate, I outlined three particular reasons for my position on this issue. I said first that I accepted that human life is different from other life forms on earth. Second, I said that on secular, philosophical grounds, I opposed the destruction of unborn children. I said that this is not a religious issue but that it is a human issue that crosses all societies and all races. In fact, one of the chief proponents of increased recognition of the rights of unborn Canadians, Dr. Bernard Nathanson, is a leading pro-life advocate in North America and opposes abortion because it is the arbitrary destruction of human life. Dr. Nathanson is an atheist.
The core of my opposition to abortion on demand is a conviction that this is a violation of the civil rights of the unborn child. In earlier speeches in the House and particularly in the speech I made on January 17, 1986, in support of a private Member's Bill I introduced, Bill C-254, I put forward the case for support for the biological reality of life before birth. I said that the unborn child can sense pain, can respond to sweetness and sourness and can move. I put forward a description of the existing legal rights of unborn children and I made it very clear to all Hon. Members that when I speak about the legal rights of unborn children, I am not introducing a novel concept. Our existing body of law, both criminal and civil, recognizes that the unborn child has legal rights that can be enforced and that are being enforced in the courts today. I outlined to Hon. Members the wide abuse of our criminal law prohibition against abortion. Notwithstanding the prohibition against abortion that exists in Canada, there is a practice which in fact is abortion on demand.
Today's debate which focuses on a motion that calls for the entrenchment of the rights of the unborn child in the Canadian Constitution is one that is being watched widely by my constituents. Before I entered the House to speak today, I discussed this issue with a rural constituent of mine, Francis De Lorey, a very strong and courageous advocate of the rights of the unborn child. I spoke with others as well.
Today I will not repeat the arguments I made on earlier occasions with respect to legal rights or medical evidence. In my view, none of that is seriously disputed. I want to take this opportunity to deal with what I believe to be a false premise on which those who advocate abortion on demand base their argument, and that premise is that we as human beings have the right to control our bodies. That argument has a certain superficial appeal, but let us think a bit about it.
What is that right to control our bodies? Does any Member of the House have the right to be kept out of jail for committing a crime? Of course not. We do not have that right because our right to control our bodies is limited by the greater social interests of enforcing certain criminal laws. That is why we can be brought before justice if we commit a crime. We can be arrested. Where is our right to control our bodies if we can be arrested? Where is our right to control our bodies if we can be physically searched? We have no absolute right to control our bodies. The right to control our bodies is a limited one. It is limited by the rights of others and by the greater social good. We see this in many situations. We cannot, for example, speak in an irresponsible way. We have free speech, but we cannot publicly condemn other people and make false statements. If we do we can be called before the civil courts and penalized.
The right to free speech is a limited right. Therefore, when I speak to the argument being put forward, which has so much superficial appeal, that a woman has the right to control her body, I think it is a false argument. It is not borne out by our legal system or by the decisions made on a daily basis concerning the rights of individuals. This Parliament and others have decided that our rights can sometimes be limited. In the case of the unborn, we are talking about the most basic of all rights, the right of that unborn child to live. It is interesting that we talk about an "unborn child". By definition a child is a person. We admit that a person exists before birth.
To conclude, it is time that we amended our Constitution to reflect the biological reality and the legal revolution taking place in our society which recognizes that biological reality. It is time that Canadian jurisprudence explicitly reflected the right of the unborn child to life. In doing so it will reflect the balancing of civil and legal rights which is an ongoing part of the evolution of our society. I urge all Hon. Members to support this motion when it comes to a vote.

subtopic: PRIVATE MEMBERS' BUSINESS-MOTIONS   THE CONSTITUTION ACT, 1982 RIGHT TO LIFE OF UNBORN HUMAN PERSONS
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I rise to express my profound concern about and opposition to the motion presented by my friend, the Hon. Member for Grey Simcoe (Mr. Mitges). I recognize the strong and deep feelings
April 2, 1987

which he brings to this question. However, I must say that I believe the adoption of this amendment to the Constitution would bring profound difficulties to the Canadian system of justice. The implications in a constitutional sense are grave and far-reaching. Most important, the implications for the women of Canada who have the right to freedom of choice on this fundamental question are very, very serious indeed.
I want to note as well that the Hon. Member has also strongly advocated that a woman who knowingly, to use his words, snuffs out a life in her womb deserves to be punished the same as anyone else convicted of premeditated murder. When asked whether that meant he would support the death penalty for women who have an abortion when their lives are not in jeopardy, his response was, and I quote, "Absolutely". Here we have a Conservative Member of Parliament advocating the death penalty for women who seek safe therapeutic abortions. I find it extraordinary that not one of that member's colleagues has stood in the House to make clear his or her opposition to this incredible suggestion. What he is saying is that women who choose to have an abortion, and it is often an agonizing personal decision, must subsequently be themselves put to death for making that decision. What an incredibly offensive and destructive attack on the women of Canada. Yet that suggestion is greeted with total silence by his colleagues in the Conservative Party.
We in the NDP agree with the concerns recently raised by the Canadian Advisory Council on the Status of Women.

The President of the National Advisory Council on the Status of Women, Mrs. Sylvia Gold, recently criticized the lack of abortion facilities across the country and the serious problems arising from this situation. She pointed out that abortion facilities in Canada had deteriorated to the point that a number of provinces were facing a real crisis. For instance, in Prince Edward Island, women cannot have abortions. In Newfoundland, there are serious problems as well. There is one doctor who agrees to perform legal abortions, but now that he is ill, there no legal abortions are being performed in Newfoundland.

I think all Canadians would agree that we as a society have to take whatever steps we can to reduce the number of abortions in Canada. That means there must be effective sex education in our schools. There must be awareness, among our young people particularly and in society generally, of birth control. Groups such as the Planned Parenthood Federation of Canada must be supported instead of having their funding cut as occurred recently.
It is interesting to note that when the Supreme Court of Canada was hearing the appeal of yet another jury acquittal of Dr. Henry Morgentaler, Mr. Justice Willard Estey mused aloud that a person would have to be affected with what he called legislative blindness not to see that there are areas in the country where there is no access to abortion whatsoever. He
Right to Life
said we have whole provinces that are carved out of the process. He asked if this was some kind of local option which has slid into the Criminal Code. Of course he was asking a rhetorical question. We know, for example, that there are nurses in the Province of Newfoundland who must spend considerable amounts of time on the telephone arranging for Newfoundland women to have their abortions in Montreal or Toronto. This happens some 40 times each month. One-third of the women of Newfoundland seeking abortions are teenagers. Many of them have never flown before or even travelled outside of the communities in which they were raised. One 14-year old was 10 weeks pregnant before she finally summoned up the courage to tell her mother. That is not an uncommon occurrence. Many Canadian women have been obliged to go to the U.S. for abortions which theoretically are medically insured, legal and available in Canada. If that is the case, why is it that in 1984 over 400 women from Prince Edward Island went to Maine for abortions? Why did 1,200 women from Ontario go to New York for the same reason? Why did 700 women from Alberta go to Washington state? Surely the time has come to recognize that this is a procedure which must be taken out of the Criminal Code as the Canadian Advisory Council on the Status of Women and the Canadian Medical Association have both recommended.
The Canadian Advisory Council on the Status of Women has three essential recommendations. First, an abortion must be recognized as a medical procedure that need not be performed in a hospital. Second, the federal and provincial Ministers of Health must approve publicly funded freestanding reproductive health clinics that would cover the whole range of the reproductive concerns of women. Third, that abortion be removed from the Criminal Code. I have tabled a Private Members' Bill in this session, just as I have in previous sessions, which would repeal the provisions of the Criminal Code dealing with abortion and leave this important decision to a woman in consultation with her doctor. By accepting these recommendations the Government would be preserving the health and well-being of women's lives.
The proposal which has been made by the Hon. Member for Grey-Simcoe to entrench this right in the Constitution of Canada could raise very serious concerns with regard to the implications of the interpretations of other legal rights in the Charter of Rights. Unfortunately, I do not have the time to pursue that particular issue, but I would like to raise briefly one other concern in this area.
There are Canadians who have recently learned of the activities of a particular organization called the Catholic Foundation for Human Life. This is a Canadian organization headed by a gentleman named David Little. Unfortunately, this organization uses treachery, deceit and dishonesty to lure pregnant women into its clinics. It suggests that if women come to their clinics they will be able to get objective advice with regard to abortions in Canada. Once they get into the office, they are instead shown films about abortion which

April 2, 1987
Right to Life
include a whole range of subjects, and it is suggested to them, for example, that they would be totally lacking in self respect if they went ahead and had a safe therapeutic abortion. It scares women and lies to women.
The Catholic Foundation for Eluman Life must be exposed for what it really is. In the United States a similar organization has been part of a congressional investigation. Action is being taken against it in the State of California for consumer fraud. In Canada other groups, including the well-known group, Birthright, have dissociated themselves from this particular organization. The founder of Birthright has said that their methods are harmful to the entire Pro-Life movement and that there is no reason to deceive at any time.
I hope that the Government and Members of Parliament will recognize that the time is long overdue for women in Canada to have access to safe therapeutic abortions, and for Canadians in general to have access to proper sex education and birth control devices. Freedom of choice must finally become a reality for all Canadian women.

subtopic: PRIVATE MEMBERS' BUSINESS-MOTIONS   THE CONSTITUTION ACT, 1982 RIGHT TO LIFE OF UNBORN HUMAN PERSONS
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I am pleased to be able to take part in this debate this afternoon. I would like to congratulate the Member for Grey-Simcoe (Mr. Mitges) who introduced this motion. I go back quite a long way on this particular issue. It is one in which I have taken a great deal of interest over the years while I have been a Member of Parliament.
In January of this year I presented a petition to the House of Commons which was presented to me by a church group in my constituency. The petition asked this House to take action to protect the lives of unborn children. The petition contained dozens of names, and I am convinced that they represent only a small percentage of the people in my constituency, let alone Canada, who are concerned about the lives of unborn children.
It has become apparent to me, through the initiatives of the Hon. Member for Grey-Simcoe, that a great many Canadians are watching this debate with a great deal of interest and hoping that some action will be taken to provide greater protection for the unborn in our nation.
I support the need for an amendment to the Charter of Rights and Freedoms to provide that "a human foetus or unborn being has the right to life, liberty and security of the person and the right not to be deprived thereof except in accordance with the principles of fundamental justice". As you will be aware, Madam Speaker, in 1969 an amendment was made to the Criminal Code which permitted abortion under three basic conditions: one, if the life of the mother is endangered by the pregnancy; two, if the abortion is performed by a medical practitioner; and three, if the abortion application is approved by a therapeutic abortion committee in an approved hospital.
While the law provides for a therapeutic abortion if the life of the mother is at risk-and I believe that if such is the case the life of the mother must take priority-the rights of the unborn child are, by the same token, too loosely protected.
Many doctors frequently ignore the life of the child when dealing with a pregnancy. It has been pointed out by other speakers that we should be dealing with a program of public education and accepting the responsibility of ensuring that unwanted pregnancies are avoided before conception. I believe that education, comprehension and prevention are certainly the most effective ways of avoiding unwanted children. I know that millions of Canadians share my view that abortion cannot be an acceptable method of birth control.
I am pleased that this motion has come before the House. In the constitutional debate of 1981 I spoke in the House of Commons and urged that the life of the unborn child be included in the Charter. As I said then, the fact that the Charter of Rights does not recognize the right to life and the rights of the unborn child is a very serious shortcoming. My position on this has not changed. I still urge the House to include such a provision in the Charter. I do not hesitate to point out that there are obviously those who disagree with me in my position on this matter. However, I have received a substantial amount of representation urging me to comply with the motion put forth by the Hon. Member for Grey-Simcoe. I believe that there is no doubt that a great many people believe that no one has the right to take the life of an innocent human being.
I would like to quote from some of the letters that I have received from my constituents. One reads:
I am in full agreement with protecting the life of the mother. However, what I see happening in our country goes far beyond that. Abortions are being performed by the thousands in our hospitals as a matter of convenience to the mothers. It is common knowledge that in most hospitals the therapeutic abortion committees rubber-stamp the requests.
Another reads:
Please take a firm stand against the awful crime of abortion and speak out for the cause of justice, life and rights of the unborn.
Yet another reads:
What kind of society are we to allow killing of the unborn, unsuspecting fetus just because of their parents' selfishness and not wanting the responsibility to care and nurture them. This is what life is all about.
I have literally dozens of letters of this nature which have come to me from my constituents. There have been many charges made by pro-abortion support groups which basically say that pro-lifers are imposing their opinions on others. I do not believe that it is really a matter of imposing opinions of morality on others, but a question of defending the rights of those who cannot defend themselves. I submit that unborn children are human beings who, by reason of their physical and mental limitations, require special safeguards and care including appropriate legal protection.
Prior to 1969, the law was steadfast in its protection of unborn children. Unfortunately, as a result of the Criminal Code amendment in 1969 there has come to pass a loss of protection for unborn children. As a result of that, there have been hundreds of thousands of lives aborted primarily as a means of birth control. This has committed society to place the quality of life of one person, that being the mother, above the
April 2, 1987

protection of the existence of another, that being the unborn child.
The most basic right of all, the right to life, has become undermined. Canada's legal system upholds the principle that no one has the right to take the life of another innocent person. What we are seeing here is that innocent human life may be taken to protect the quality of life of a person more powerful, a person with choice. I submit that we can no longer, as a society, permit that kind of focus in laying the ground work and rules for what we know is just not the proper position for a caring society to take.

subtopic: PRIVATE MEMBERS' BUSINESS-MOTIONS   THE CONSTITUTION ACT, 1982 RIGHT TO LIFE OF UNBORN HUMAN PERSONS
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I am honoured to have the opportunity to participate in this debate on the motion of my colleague, the Hon. Member for Grey Simcoe (Mr. Mitges) to amend Section 7 of the Canadian Charter of Rights in order that human foetus or unborn beings are given full protection of the law. Since 1969, when the Criminal Code was amended, Canada has been split into two distinct factions on the question of abortion. I strongly believe that life begins at conception and therefore must be protected, as my seat-mate, the Elon. Member for Cape Breton Highlands-Canso (Mr. O'Neil) so eloquently pointed out earlier on.
The question of the rights of the unborn has been with us since man has been able to affect his environment. Once man learned he could manipulate his surroundings and was able to apply his knowledge to further his existence, the question of life became his focal point. The Bible is very explicit on life. Deuteronomy 30: 19 states:
I call heaven and earth to witness against you this day, that I have set before
you life and death, blessing and curse: therefore choose life, that you and your
descendants may live, loving the Lord your God.
All major religions have made the protection of life a major part of their beliefs. "Choose life" is what the motion before us today is all about. By entrenching the right to life of a human foetus, or the unborn, we will finally bestow the fundamental principles of justice on the innocent who have yet to be born.
My focus on this motion will be from a contemporary and scientific perspective, because I feel that science is much easier to understand and accept for most people as proof that life begins at conception and, as such, the rights of the unborn must be protected in the same way as our own rights.
Advances in science such as ultrasound and photographic histeroscopy have provided the solid evidence that life begins at conception, as Dr. Nathanson showed Members of Parliament on the Hill this week with his film Eclipse of Reason. The question as to when life becomes human is, never. Like life, humanity is continuous. Intrinsically and extrinsically, the sperm, ovum, the zygote and all the cells, tissue and stages which arise from the zygote, are human. None of them can every be categorized as belonging to any other species. Human life is not started, it is transmitted. There is no instant or
Right to Life
interval of time between fertilization and birth when the unborn offspring is anything but human.
Flanagan writes in The First Nine Months-. "From the first hour the human cells are distinctly human". The medical profession is in complete agreement with this statement. The international code of medical ethics states: "A doctor must always bear in mind the importance of preserving human life from the time of conception until death". Similarly, the declaration of Geneva reads: "I will maintain the utmost respect for human life from the time of conception".
It is apparent that human life is recognized as beginning at conception, and abortion must then be the taking of human life. An editorial in the pro-abortion journal California Medicine admits that abortion is the taking of human life. The editorial states:
The reverence of each and every human life has been the keystone of the
western medicine, and is the ethic which has caused physicians to try to
preserve, protect, repair, prolong and enhance every human life.
Since the old ethic, fortunately, has not yet been fully displaced, it has been necessary to separate the idea of abortion from the idea of killing, which continues to be socially abhorrent. The result has been a curious avoidance of the scientific fact, readily accepted, that human life begins at conception and is continuous, whether intra or extra-uterine, until death.
The considerable semantic gymnastics which are required to rationalize abortion as anything but the taking of human life would be ludicrous if they were not often put forth under socially impeccable auspices. It is suggested that this schizophrenic sort of subterfuge is necessary because, while a new ethic is apparently being accepted, the old ethic, fortunately, has not yet been rejected.
The Pro-abortion Journal pulls no punches. It recognizes that the concept that life begins at conception is the tenet in which the majority of the population still believes. The only way to counter this is to describe abortion as socially acceptable and as a means for a woman to control her body. There is no thought given to the innocent life which is being barbarical-ly terminated. Yet abortions continue to be carried out at an average of 60,000 a year. Stop and think, Madam Speaker, 60,000 innocent lives are terminated each year in Canada for no reason whatsoever.
One may recognize that in some cases an abortion must be performed to preserve the physical health of the mother, but the overwhelming majority of abortions are made for purely social reasons. One asks how a human who possesses the capacities for consciousness, rationality and cognition makes such drastic decisions when it concerns human life. There is no thought given to the moral and physical obligation which is owed to the innocent life. Only the self is considered when such decisions are made.
Abortion is becoming the main means of contraception. Abortion has allowed individuals the freedom from responsibility for their actions. Individuals must accept responsibility for

April 2, 1987
Right to Life
their sexual acts. The end result of intercourse, with ensuing pregnancy, should be acceptance of the unborn child as a unique gift. Avoidance of pregnancy by responsible use of our sexuality is the only alternative to abortion. In today's society, there should be no excuse for an unwanted pregnancy. Abortion cheapens the value of life. The ability to terminate a pregnancy with minimum discomfort gives individuals a lax attitude towards the sanctity of life. The greater ease with which abortion is conducted will serve to further desensitize the population to disregard the value of human life.
Respect for life is one of the cornerstones of our civilization. Any assaults on humans who are already born result in severe penalties on the perpetrators. Yet many in our society condone the barbaric acts inflicted on unborn human beings. We cannot have a double standard towards life. Either life is accepted as sacred for all or society runs the risk of cheapening the value of human life.
The main argument used to deny the unborn human the full protection of our laws is, meekly, that a foetus is not human because it cannot think. However, scientific evidence, to which I referred earlier, is clear that life begins when a sperm fertilizes an egg cell. Most pregnancies are not even detected until the sixth week. By then the baby's heart has been beating for three weeks, brain waves can be read, the nervous system has been complete for about two weeks and he or she is about to begin moving, although the mother will not feel it for another three and a half months.
There are on average over 20,000 abortions every year in Canada under nine weeks. Yet the foetus's brain is registering activity. The presence of the brain activity should be a major deterrent against abortion. Brain activity clearly indicates the individual's humanity, recognized even until death. By the eighth week the baby's skeleton, head, face, arms, legs, fingers, with finger prints, toes, circulatory and major muscle systems are complete. Yet abortions are done.
By the twelfth week, the baby already shows a distinct individuality in both appearance and behaviour, with the facial expressions resembling those of his or her parents. During the period between nine to 12 weeks an average of 35,000 abortions are carried out each year. However, abortions do not stop at 12 weeks. There are each year an average of 6,500 abortions carried out on unborn children over 16 weeks. In fact, there is no legal time limit on abortion. An abortion can be carried out at any stage of the pregnancy, up to the ninth month. This must be stopped.
With all the scientific evidence that has been accumulated and our moral history, it is clear that life must be protected. An unborn child presently has no protection. A criminal proven guilty has more protection under the law than the unborn. Just stop and think about it-a guilty criminal has more protection than an unborn human being. The unborn are innocent. Yet their fate is determined by very little or no consideration at all. Compare the consideration given the
unborn to that a criminal receives in our justice system and it becomes apparent that something is very wrong with our morality.
Once life has begun it has the same right to reach its natural end. By destroying life to ensure one's economic and social success the human race is losing its honour and dignity. The human race which is now reaching for the stars must not be allowed to regress to the level where life has only a relative value.
I urge all Members of the House to give the unborn the right to survive. The Bible, and now science, have provided us with concrete evidence that life begins at conception. I will be supporting the motion which is before us. I urge all Members to do the same.

subtopic: PRIVATE MEMBERS' BUSINESS-MOTIONS   THE CONSTITUTION ACT, 1982 RIGHT TO LIFE OF UNBORN HUMAN PERSONS
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I am very pleased to be entering into this debate this afternoon to put my thoughts and my position on abortion clearly on the record. I would like to acknowledge the contribution made by the Hon. Member for Grey-Simcoe (Mr. Mitges) for the introduction of this motion. I would also like to acknowledge the amendment, which was ruled on on January 26, 1987, which added the word "human" to this resolution.
I believe that the addition of the word "human" was very important to the wording of the motion. I think that one of the reasons people are advocating the pro-choice position is that they have tried for some time now to de-humanize the unborn child. By referring to the unborn child as a "foetus" they somehow indicate that it is something less than a person. There has never been any doubt in my mind that the unborn child is a human person and becomes one at conception.
Our individual biological system begins at conception and will end at death. It provides us with the very obvious fact that life is a continuum. At all stages of this continuum we are human, as the science of genetics can document. Thus our humanity does not depend on our size, our stage of development or our place of residence. Calling human beings "embryos" or "foetuses" serves the same purpose as calling them "adolescents" or "adults". These scientific terms are used to indicate where a person is in his or her development. They were never meant to imply that the unborn child is not human. As the infant is different from the adolescent in terms of development and dependence, so the foetus is different from the infant. Yet all are genetically human and therefore persons. When we consider that at the moment we were conceived our blood group, the colour of our eyes, the colour of our skin, our sex and all our inherited qualities were actually already determined, would it not then be logical to conclude that since we had our own blood group, the colour of our eyes and our sex determined that we began to exist at conception?
Another commonly held myth centres around the belief that whatever is legal is moral-in this case abortion. We all know, if we look back in history, that there were some regimes which tried to legalize, and in fact did legalize, things that they were doing but things that were very immoral. Probably the most
April 2, 1987

common example of this is what took place in Germany during the Second World War. Although Hitler did legalize what took place, it was certainly very immoral. It was roundly condemned by other nations of the world.
I think that most adults in Canada would realize that abortion is killing a human being. I understand that in the United States there is a law that states if a person is convicted of destroying the egg of a bald eagle then that person can be fined up to $5,000. I am sure that everyone understands the thinking behind this law. It is that if one destroys a fertilized eagle's egg then one has destroyed an eaglet since a fertilized egg represents a potential eaglet.
I think it is also important to realize that this debate really began in 1969 when some amendments were made to the Criminal Code. What really happened in 1969 is that Parliament completely replaced judicial control after the fact by medical control before the fact. This is the real change in the law as it concerns abortion. Even though the number of therapeutic abortions has increased significantly since the reform of 1969, it is not because the legal criteria allowing abortions was liberalized but because it was decided that the responsibility for applying the legislation would rest with the medical profession. Parliament did not, as some people still believe, liberalize the substantive conditions for access to therapeutic abortion by allowing it either on demand or for various other reasons such as having an abnormal child, incest, rape and so on. It merely removed the determination from the courts by means of a purely procedural technique which entrusted to an administrative body, in this case a therapeutic abortion committee, the task of judging whether such an abortion is necessary, while taking into consideration the traditional criteria of the danger such an operation could represent to the life or health of the woman.
There are some other interesting facts regarding abortion that I would like to read into the record. On January 30, 1984, while addressing the National Religious Broadcasters Convention the President of the United States, Ronald Reagan, said:
-medical science doctors confirm that when the lives of the unborn are
snuffed out, they often feel pain, pain that is long and agonizing.
This statement immediately provoked ridicule from many columnists and reporters who said things such as "appalling", "dubious fact from his store of demi-knowledge", "outright demagoguery" and "there is no evidence". One columnist even suggested that this was a "fact" culled from an anti-abortion journal. This revelation of the fact of foetal pain could not go unchallenged by pro-abortionists as research indicates that the more aware one is of the facts about life in the womb the less likely one is to tolerate abortion. Public knowledge of foetal pain, and everything else that really happens in abortion, would strip pro-abortionists of their self-appointed mantle of compassion.
As a result of this statement by the President, Dr. Irvin Nichols, Director of Practice Activities for the American College of Obstetricians and Gynecologists, purporting to
Right to Life
speak for the association's 24,000 members, supplied The New York Times with this statement:
We are unaware of any evidence of any kind that would substantiate a claim that pain is perceived by the foetus.
This statement was published in The New York Times of January 31, 1984. It prompted 26 other physicians, all specialists in the field, two of whom were past presidents of the American College, to denounce Dr. Nichols' official answer. They wrote the President the following:
Over the last 18 years, real time ultrasonography, fetoscopy, study of the foetal EKG and foetal EEG have demonstrated the remarkable responsiveness of the human foetus to pain, touch and sound . .. The ability to feel pain and respond to it is clearly not a phenomenon that develops de nova at birth. Indeed, much of enlightened modern obstetrical practice and procedure seeks to minimize sensory deprivation of, and sensory insult to, the foetus during, at and after birth ... Mr. President, in drawing the attention to the capability of the human foetus to feel pain, you stand on firmly established ground.
At the First International Conference on Abortion held in Washington, D.C., in 1967, world authorities in genetics, biochemistry, biology, medicine, law, ethics and the social sciences concluded that human life begins at conception. Their almost unanimous conclusion, 19 to one, was made as follows:
The majority of our group could find no point in time between the union of sperm and egg, or at least the blastos stage and the birth of the infant, at which point we could say that this was not a human life.
Dr. Bernard Nathanson of New York, a former leading abortionist in the United States who presided over more than 60,000 abortions, came to the conclusion, with the use of ultrasound technology, that the foetus is an identifiable human being.
Dr. Heather Morris of Women's College Hospital in Toronto has said:
The unborn human is still a human life, and not all the wishful thinking of those advocating repeal of the abortion laws can alter this. Only those who are irrational or ignorant of science doubt that when a human sperm fertilizes a human ovum, a new human being is created.
We are also heartened when we have decisions such as the one handed down by Justice Sandra Day O'Connor, a member of the U.S. Supreme Court, in her judgment of June, 1983, wherein she stated:
I believe that the state's interest in protecting potential human life exists throughout pregnancy. Recent studies have demonstrated increasingly earlier foetal viability. It is certainly reasonable to believe that foetal viability in the first trimester of pregnancy may be possible in the not-too-distant future.
I should also like to point out to my constituents, Madam Speaker, with some pride, that on this difficult issue, I was prepared to make a choice, a choice that I believe is the right choice, and to stand up in this honourable Chamber and let that choice be known.
I should like to quote some words of the late Right Hon. Member from Prince Albert, Mr. Diefenbaker, who was well known in this Chamber, when he said: "I may sometimes have been on the wrong side of an issue, but I have never been on the side of wrong."

April 2, 1987
Right to Life
In my estimation, Madam Speaker, abortion is this type of issue.
I should also like to quote Edmund Burke, who said: "All that is required for evil to triumph, is for good men to do nothing." I think in this particular instance we could say: "for good parliamentarians to do nothing".
Every hour, eight unborn Canadians needlessly suffer an agonizing death. If we avert our gaze and close our ears to their "silent screams", can we claim to be compassionate human beings? The answer is obvious.
The unborn cannot help themselves, except as their tortured bodies offer evidence that moves those already born. If the suffering of the defenceless does not arouse our compassion and move us to act on their behalf, nothing ever will.
Madam Speaker, on behalf of the over 60,000 Canadian children who are aborted each year in Canada, I urge, not only Members of this honourable House, but all Canadians, to support the motion introduced by the Hon. Member for Grey-Simcoe.

subtopic: PRIVATE MEMBERS' BUSINESS-MOTIONS   THE CONSTITUTION ACT, 1982 RIGHT TO LIFE OF UNBORN HUMAN PERSONS
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, before entering the debate proper on this important issue, I should like to read into the record a letter that was sent to me by Sister Marie Philippe, who is in charge of the Grey Nuns Provincial House in the Town of Fort Smith, in my constituency.
It reads:
Dear Sir:
I am writing this letter to you concerning the Private Member's Bill of Gus Mitges MP. His Bill proposes that section 7 of the Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms should be amended to read as follows:
"Everyone, including the human foetus or unborn being has the right to Life, Liberty and security of person and the right not to be deprived thereof except in accordance with the principles of fundamental justice."
I wish to make it clear that I totally support this initiative and amendment and respectfully request that you do the same.
And it is signed by Sister Marie Philippe.
Madam Speaker, I have received many letters, not only from other Grey Nuns but from people of many walks of life in my constituency, on this subject. Of course, I have to point out that I have received a few which take the opposite point of view to that which is set out in this particular letter. However, if the amount of mail in favour of this Bill is any measure, the Hon. Member for Grey-Simcoe (Mr. Mitges) would certainly seem to have the support of the majority of my constituents. I congratulate him for bringing to the floor of the House of Commons such an important subject. It is a subject that will require much more debate before amendments to the Criminal Code that meet with general acceptance by the Canadian population can be brought forward.
As Members of Parliament, we are all, at frequent intervals, asked to expound on our views on this subject, and I, like most other MPs, am pleased to do so.
My views are based on the concept of the sanctity of human life. I am of the view that abortions are not to take place except in certain very special circumstances. Exceptions that I can think of would include cases where the life or health of the mother is at stake, or in cases of pregnancy due to rape.
Abortions certainly ought not to be used as a form of birth control. I recall some statistics for the City of Toronto, where the number of abortions performed exceeds the number of live births. That is something that is wrong; that is something that is not acceptable.
I have some doubt as to the extent to which legislators' private moral concepts ought to be imposed, by law, on the public at large-and if time permits, I shall get back to that idea a little later in my presentation.
We certainly ought not to support the idea espoused by the New Democratic Party, one of abortion on demand. Quite frankly, I am appalled that a national political Party in Canada could take such a callous attitude toward human life.
I know that, generally speaking, Conservatives believe in individual rights-and surely each foetus is an individual; and 1 know that my socialist friends believe more in group rights, rather than in individual rights. But I cannot see how that would lead them to take the view that abortion on demand is something that should be permitted.
If one takes the Conservative view, if one believes in individual rights, in individual freedoms, one has to be very concerned with the whole question of abortion and what we are doing to so many unborn Canadians. I shouldn't think that the NDP would be so unmindful of those rights.
This question is one that is correctly argued on moral and ethical grounds. I think there is a moral and ethical basis to most of the laws of Canada. We cannot disregard those grounds. They are of paramount importance in a debate such as this.
Because morals and ethics are so intertwined with the question, the religious community takes a great interest in it. There was an article in today's Globe and Mail that pointed this out. The hidden suggestion in the article is that there was something wrong with that; that there was something wrong with people with firm and strong religious beliefs entering into this argument in the way that they do.
I do not take that view at all. That is why I started off this afternoon with a letter that had been written by a very well respected Grey Nun from my constituency. I think it is good that the church, and members of the church, takes such an interest in this question.
But apart from that, I feel that there are important practical reasons to discourage the practice of abortion in Canada. In my opinion, Canada remains under-populated. We have 25 million people in a country with an area of something like 4 million square miles. We have lots of land in which to expand. We can add many, many more people to our population.
April 2, 1987

In fact, the birth rate rate now is less than 2.1 per cent, the level necessary to keep the population stable; it is down to around 1.7 per cent. In my opinion, it ought to be national policy to keep up the birth rate, thereby adding to the population of Canada.
I notice, Madam Speaker, that my time is rapidly expiring. I hope that the few ideas and thoughts I have been able to put on the record with respect to this most important subject will prove to be of some value.

subtopic: PHARMACEUTICAL INDUSTRY-AFFIDAVIT OF CHAIRMAN OF U.S. GENERIC PHARMACEUTICAL INDUSTRY ASSOCIATION. (B) REQUEST THAT CANADIAN AMBASSADOR APPEAR BEFORE COMMITTEE
PHARMACEUTICAL INDUSTRY-AFFIDAVIT OF CHAIRMAN OF U.S. GENERIC PHARMACEUTICAL INDUSTRY ASSOCIATION. (B) REQUEST THAT CANADIAN AMBASSADOR APPEAR BEFORE COMMITTEE
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, on March 27, 1987, I put a question to the Right Hon. Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Clark) regarding an affidavit of Mr. William Haddad, Chairman of the Generic Pharmaceutical Industry Association of the United States which I had introduced the previous day. He asserted that in his deliberations with the Canadian Ambassador in Washington, when they met with Mr. Pratt, the President's Chairman of the Advisory Committee on Trade Negotiations, as well as the Chairman and Chief Executive Officer of one of the largest multinational drug companies in the world with profits for the first nine months in excess of $500 million, it was reported by the Canadian Ambassador that he could not determine whether or not Mr. Pratt was representing the interests of the United States and/or the interests of his own multinational corporation.
The Secretary of State for External Affairs took the opportunity to say that the affidavit was false. I then asked him to explain to the House what measures he undertook with the Canadian Ambassador in Washington in order to arrive at that particular conclusion.
For whatever reasons, the Secretary of State for External Affairs chose not to tell us in any detail what undertakings he
Adjournment Debate
took. Suffice it to say, from his perspective he said: "I spoke with the Canadian Ambassador and I believe him".
That is not sufficient. 1 would have thought that the Secretary of State for External Affairs would have outlined some detail of the investigations he undertook on behalf of the Canadian Government, in order to clarify some of the assertions regarding the generic industry in the United States as well as here in Canada in the duly notarized and signed affidavit which was witnessed by legal counsel.
In a supplementary question to the Minister I asked to have the Canadian Ambassador appear before the Standing Committee on External Affairs in order that we would have an opportunity to examine first hand the representations he had received from the United States Government, as well as from individuals in the United States pharmaceutical industry.
The reason or the rationale for that is that the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs and International Trade (Mr. Andre) has persistently and consistently, inside and outside the House, said that he has not received any representations whatsoever from the United States Government and/or the pharmaceutical industry in the United States. We believe that to be patently false. We believe that some strong representations have been made to the Canadian Government. We know that the multinational corporations have lobbied long and hard to have changes and amendments made to our Patent Act.
For some reason the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs, aided and abetted by the Secretary of State for External Affairs, refuses to acknowledge that those representations have in fact been made.
1 have concluded from my investigations, from my knowledge of the file, and from the refusal of the Government to allow individuals to appear before standing committees to have the matter clarified once and for all, that the Government has something to hide when it comes to pharmaceuticals and the prices of drugs. It is clear that the policy now being put forward by the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs was not written in Canada but in major cities in the United States, the homeland of the multinational drug companies. In my view the Secretary of State for External Affairs is being very catty with regard to the entire issue.
Furthermore, it is extremely interesting to note that when Members of the Opposition question the Government and the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) with regard to the policy on Bill C-22 or amendments to the Patent Act, the Prime Minister never avails himself of the opportunity to stand in his place and respond. I am not suggesting for one moment that there is anything wrong with that, but it is an interesting observation that if the Prime Minister believes so strongly in the legislation being advocated by his colleague in the Cabinet, he will certainly want to avail himself of every opportunity to buttress, enhance and support his colleague.

April 2, 1987
Adjournment Debate
The facts are very clear. They are as follows: Canadians, as a result of Bill C-22, will pay substantially increased costs for prescription drugs. There is no enforceable guarantee or commitment regarding research and development. There is no enforceable guarantee regarding the creation of new jobs pursuant to Bill C-22. What is obvious to every reasonable, ordinary Canadian is that this legislation is being promoted by multinational corporations which have won their way into the hearts of the Prime Minister, the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs and, of course, the Secretary of State for External Affairs.
I hope the Parliamentary Secretary will come clean with Canadians as to why we are being forced to swallow this legislation written in another sovereign country, namely the United States.

speakeroldname: Mr. Roger Clinch (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister for External Relations):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for External Relations
subtopic: PHARMACEUTICAL INDUSTRY-AFFIDAVIT OF CHAIRMAN OF U.S. GENERIC PHARMACEUTICAL INDUSTRY ASSOCIATION. (B) REQUEST THAT CANADIAN AMBASSADOR APPEAR BEFORE COMMITTEE
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I trust I will be able to clarify some of the allegations made by the Hon. Member for Cape Breton-East Richmond (Mr. Dingwall).
With regard to the affidavit sworn by Mr. Haddad on March 23, 1987, officials of the Department of External Affairs in Ottawa have been in contact with officials at the Canadian Embassy in Washington and, through them, with Ambassador Gotlieb. As a result, it has been ascertained that the contents of the affidavit do not conform to the recollection of the meeting held by the Ambassador and the Canadian officials who were present. Embassy officials meet frequently with representatives of special interest groups, like Mr. Haddad of the generic industry and Mr. Pratt of the brand name drug manufacturers as part of their normal responsibilities. There was no confusion at any time as to Mr. Pratt's role. His representations on this issue were made in his private capacity as chairman and chief executive officer of Pfizer Inc., and at no time did Mr. Pratt speak, or purport to speak, on behalf of the Reagan administration concerning Bill C-22.
As we have said before, the amendments reflect a careful balance between the concerns of the pharmaceutical industry, Canadian industrial development goals and the need to control health care costs. They are based primarily on domestic considerations and will increase research and development investment and create employment in a vital high-tech industry.

subtopic: FISHERIES-REQUEST THAT MINISTER MEET REPRESENTATIVES OF STAR-KIST PLANT WORKERS. (B) HERRING-ROE FISHERYLEASING OF LICENCES
FISHERIES-REQUEST THAT MINISTER MEET REPRESENTATIVES OF STAR-KIST PLANT WORKERS. (B) HERRING-ROE FISHERYLEASING OF LICENCES
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, on March 3 of this year I asked the Hon. Minister of Fisheries and Oceans (Mr. Siddon) when he was going to put an end to the practice now prevalent on the Pacific Coast of leasing herring licences and doubling herring licences. The Minister replied that the herring industry advisory board did not recommend changes this year. I would like to point out that organizations representing over 90 per cent of the same fishermen in British Columbia, the people
most vitally involved with the herring fishery, have recommended that those practices be ended. I refer specifically to the United Fishermen and Allied Workers' Union, the Native Brotherhood of British Columbia and the Prince Rupert Fishermen's Guild.
Theoretically, the licences available for herring fishing are non-transferable. There are a number of ways of circumventing this, the most common of which is probably the 99-year lease. There is no requirement for licence-holders to own vessels. A practice has developed of renting licences to speculators and companies. Gordon Bisaro, a lawyer specializing in fisheries, pointed out that in 1986, the standard rate for a 99-year lease on a herring gill-net licence was $18,000 and on a seine licence it was $125,000. This year, the going rate is $45,000 for a gill-net and $300,000 for a seine. This amount of money is being paid for a licence for which the licence-holder had to pay the Government $200 in the case of a gill-net licence and $2,000 in the case of a seine licence.
The trade in these licences has gone completely crazy. The rental charged for a gill-net licence for a single season is $10,000 and it is between $50,000 and $100,000 for a seine licence. Some of the people who own or control these licences through 99-year leases have no connection whatsoever with the herring-roe industry or with the fishing industry itself for that matter. In some cases, it makes more sense for a licence-holder to sit on the beach and rent out his licence for $100,000, letting someone else do the work while he collects the money.
In addition to that, in 1981 the Government introduced a system of area licences. The coast has been broken down into several different areas and a licence covers just one of those areas. In recent years, there has been a doubling of licences. One person might control licences for more than one area. In order to pay for this, the people who work as crew members on seine boats are required to bid in for their jobs. In effect, they are required to buy their jobs. This is an immoral and uneconomical situation.
Because of the doubling of licences, many people who would traditionally work in the herring industry are unable to because other people control licences for more than one area. This year, up to 400 people who would traditionally work in the herring industry are sitting on the beach because they cannot afford to pay anywhere between $3,000 and $10,000 just for a chance to work on one of those boats as a crew member. That is a completely immoral situation.
As I pointed out, the organizations that represent the majority of the seine fishermen in British Columbia, the United Fishermen and Allied Workers' Union, the Native Brotherhood of British Columbia and the Prince Rupert Fishermen's Guild, have all indicated that this situation should be changed. The Minister has known about this problem since at least January 14, 1983, when he sent a letter to Bill Procopation, the business agent for the United Fishermen and Allied Workers' Union. The letter reads as follows:
April 2, 1987

Dear Bill:
Thank you for sending me a copy of your letter to the Minister of Fisheries
on the subject of roe herring licensing.
The two-licence system definitely raises some serious concerns, and it is a
matter of interest to a number of Progressive Conservative M.P.'S.
It then goes on to talk about some correspondence he has had. It is signed:
Yours very truly,
Tom Siddon, MP Richmond-South Delta
That was when he was in opposition. He was aware then of the very serious nature of the problem. He pointed out that other Conservative MPs were aware of it as well. Yet so far no action has been taken. We have to ask why.
The Government was elected on the basis of its promise to create jobs. It has instead allowed the loss of jobs in the herring industry to continue.
I would like to emphasize the fact that this is a growing problem. In 1983 there were 30 doubled licences. That increased to 54 in 1984. By 1985 there were 75. It dropped slightly in 1986 to 67. This year there are at least 79. We do not know where the people who have the leases on those licences are located. In some cases it is speculators, in others it is the companies. The purpose of area licensing when it was introduced in 1981 was to prevent boats from racing from one area to another. It was an attempt to share the wealth and organize orderly management of the resource. However, it is very obvious from the statistics I have presented here, and which members of the industry have presented to the Minister, that the situation is not working the way theory says it should. It has completely broken down. It is working to the detriment of the industry and the workers.
I want to emphasize that there is something wrong with an advisory process when the largest organizations representing the fishermen on the coast cannot get the Minister to act to solve an obvious problem which he has known about for four
Adjournment Debate
years. He says the Herring Advisory Council has not recommended action for this year. However, it is absolutely critical that action be taken and that this situation not be repeated in the herring industry next year.

subtopic: FISHERIES-REQUEST THAT MINISTER MEET REPRESENTATIVES OF STAR-KIST PLANT WORKERS. (B) HERRING-ROE FISHERYLEASING OF LICENCES
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, as the Hon. Member pointed out, when this double licensing plan went into effect it was intended to prevent boats from moving from one area to another and infringing upon the rights of others. It was meant to spread the resource around, share the wealth, and allow for some management of the stocks. We know there were some problems with the plan at the outset. I know the Minister is very concerned about this.
With reference to the matter of the advisory process, I am in complete agreement with the member that the process must be made to work. The people concerned must be able to sit down with officials from the Department of Fisheries and Oceans and the Minister in order to come up with some recommendations acceptable to all concerned. The concern of this Government is to consult with the fishermen and others concerned on the West Coast and come up with some way of resolving the problem to everyone's satisfaction.
I know the Hon. Member has been very patient in this regard and I know he will continue to be patient and make his representations and those of his colleagues known to the Minister. I am sure the Minister will be willing to sit down with the Hon. Member and other interested parties in order to resolve the problem through the advisory and consultative process.
